detail.abstract: Online product reviews influence the choices people make while shopping. Customers often depend on ratings and written feedback before buying a product, but this system becomes unreliable when reviews are fake or intentionally misleading. Fake reviews may be posted to promote a product, harm a competitor, increase ratings, or create a false image of customer satisfaction. Detecting such reviews is challenging because fake reviews can look very similar to genuine ones. They may use realistic language, strong emotions, productrelated words, and believable experiences. For this reason, fake-review detection cannot depend only on sentiment or grammar. It may also require information about reviewer behaviour, review timing, rating patterns, text similarity, and possible coordination among reviewers. This paper reviews important research in fake-review and opinion-spam detection and proposes a practical machine-learning framework for future implementation. The framework includes dataset collection, data cleaning, text preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, prediction, explainability, human moderation, and continuous monitoring. It also discusses the use of classical machine-learning models, such as Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machines, along with more advanced NLP approaches based on transformer models. The study is conceptual and based on existing literature. No new model has been trained or tested in this paper. Therefore, it does not claim a new accuracy score or experimental result. Instead, it presents an evaluation plan that can be used in future work, including precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, inference time, robustness, and cross-dataset performance.

detail.abstract: Provenance can establish how a record was produced without establishing that its contents or subsequent interpretations are correct. This paper specifies an evidence architecture that separates versioned source objects, deterministic validation, AI-generated interpretations, and human review. Blockchain is assigned an optional anchoring role; the implemented prototype uses a signed centralized append-only log. Exact object references, domainseparated signatures, correction-driven review invalidation, and replayable decisions make the boundary between record integrity and claim support explicit. A frozen descriptive evaluation applied two prompt-and-gate configurations to 20 microgrid household groups under valid evidence, missing evidence, and prompt injection, producing 120 recorded attempts. Of these, 112 outputs satisfied the authoritative schema, but none of 80 substantive answers was fully supported; none of 61 finite numerical values matched the reference within tolerance. Uniform replay of the full checker admitted eight outputs, all abstentions, including five unnecessary refusals. These findings show why schema conformance, citation validity, and gate admission must be reported separately from supported task completion. The contribution is a concrete provenance and evaluation workflow with inspectable failure cases. The study does not establish useful semantic or regulatory reasoning, human-review effectiveness, or a performance advantage for blockchain.

detail.abstract: Paper presented at 2026 TPRC | The rapid proliferation of generative AI is fundamentally reshaping the U.S. legal and regulatory landscape, introducing significant uncertainty for developers and policymakers navigating the complex interplay of federal directives and state-level initiatives. Despite the growing body of literature on AI's technical vulnerabilities, there remains a critical gap in understanding the compliance environment and the efficacy of current state-level regulatory responses. This paper employs a qualitative legal and policy analysis of 200 enacted state bills collected between October and December 2025 to examine: areas of emerging state consensus on AI privacy; the consequences of polycentric compliance; and existing governance gaps. Our analysis reveals four persistent gaps in the U.S. regulatory architecture: a lack of explicit oversight regarding inferential analytics; limited remedies for algorithmic bias; the exclusion of emerging risks (e.g., deepfakes and synthetic media); and highly heterogeneous enforcement mechanisms that rely on varying degrees of regulatory and private oversight. These governance gaps contribute to a fragmented compliance environment that disproportionately impacts vulnerable populations and undermines accountability. This study ultimately highlights the urgent need for harmonized frameworks that transcend the limitations of current polycentric approaches to ensure equitable and accountable AI governance.

detail.abstract: AI explainability in organizations remains elusive because research often separates the objective design of AI from people's subjective perception of it. From a sociotechnical perspective, we develop the AI Match Framework (AIMF), which crosses three objective designs (predefined function AI, end-product generative AI, and machine learning AI) with three subjective perceptions (mechanical AI, thinking AI, and knowledge generation AI). We define AI explainability as people's explaining behavior grounded in system-provided explanations and introduce the perception-design gap as the central construct. Building on research on AI's learning, inscrutability, and autonomy, we propose that matches yield reasonable automation, information processing, or knowledge generation; over-attribution wastes explanation effort; and under-attribution weakens oversight, fosters automation bias, and heightens ethical risk. We extend AIMF to composite AI systems, stakeholder processes, procedural explainability, and AI agents, and outline implications for management, governance, and research.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms monetize engagement, but not all engagement is good for consumers. The same information that lets a platform recommend content a consumer enjoys also lets it recommend content that engages but enrages him. We study how privacy policies and platform commitment affect this conflict. We show when a government requirement to offer privacy does not strictly benefit consumers; when privacy benefits consumers and the platform offers it voluntarily; and when the platform and a majority of consumers prefer mandatory privacy. Under the profit-maximizing commitment to a recommender system, the platform still prioritizes the most enraging content, all else equal.

detail.abstract: Security assurance commonly records whether a control has been adopted and rarely whether it operates. This paper proposes an instrument for separating the two and applies it to every domain in three defined populations. The Control Operating State scale is a six-state ordinal ladder, from Absent to Owned, in which each state carries its own evidence requirement. The Control Operation Gap (COG) is the share of a population at State 2 or above minus the share at State 4 or above. Where State 4 cannot be observed, the share configured to enforce is used as a ceiling on operation, so every reported gap is a floor. The index is applied to DMARC email authentication across 18,393 domains drawn in full from three United States federal registries: FDIC-insured institutions with assets between $100 million and $10 billion (n = 3,492), HRSA health centers and look-alike sites (n = 1,915), and five domain types of the CISA .gov registry (n = 12,986). Adoption ranges from 56.1 percent to 88.6 percent across the three populations, a spread of 32.5 points, while the gap ranges only from 20.6 to 22.0. Federal executive branch domains, the one population subject to a binding directive, show adoption of 91.1 percent and a gap of 1.8. The contrast holds when the analysis is restricted to domains that publish a mail exchanger (3.5 against 27.3 for the rest of .gov), although the directive cannot be separated from central administration of the domain space. Supplementary measures show that 2.7 percent of domains publish a domain-verification record for one of three AI vendors tested, while 1.3 percent of testable domains resolve at least one of six tested AIrelated host labels, and that adjacent controls outside the principal DMARC measure, such as MTA-STS (1.4 to 1.9 percent), are seldom deployed. The results are consistent with assurance practices that count adoption and do not inspect operating state.

detail.abstract:
LLM-generated strategic advice may differ in how broadly it represents the competitive environment, yet the extent and structure of this coverage remain insufficiently established. This article assesses industry-structure coverage in LLM-generated strategic advice using Porter's Five Forces as the criterion domain. 

Comparative quantitative content analysis was applied to 192 standardised conversations comprising 1,920 LLM replies. Four LLM models (ChatGPT-5.5, Claude Haiku-4.5/Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3.1/3.5 and Grok-4.3.), two response modes (instant and thinking) and four Porter competitive strategies were examined. Industry-structure coverage was measured using a 25-indicator adaptation of INDUSTRUCT and aggregated into force-specific rates and the Five Forces Coverage Score (FFCS). 

Overall coverage was limited and strongly uneven. Rivalry and supplier power were represented far more often than buyer power, while other two forces-entry and substitutes-were almost absent. Coverage did not differ significantly across LLM families or response modes, whereas Porter competitive strategy showed a strong effect, with lower coverage in differentiation-oriented conditions. 

The findings indicate that broad industry-structure representation cannot be inferred from general strategic capability alone and support explicitly structuring all five forces when a comprehensive microenvironment analysis is required.

detail.abstract: Two questions increasingly intersect in the study of AI-enabled science. The first is whether artificial intelligence changes the rate and cumulativeness of validated discovery. The second is whether any observed change constitutes a new scientific regime rather than a larger volume of activity inside the old one. Companion work develops, respectively, a discovery-rate framework linked to longevity escape velocity and an emergence-adjudication architecture that separates novelty, predictive structure, coarse-grained dynamics, causal contribution, multidirectional causal closure, and computational shortcutability. This paper develops the statistical-mechanical language connecting those two programmes. Scientific discovery is represented as a finite, open, adaptive system with many interacting units. The framework defines microstates, macrostates, ensembles, candidate order parameters, correlation scales, response functions, coarse-graining maps, renormalisation-group-inspired relevance, finitesize scaling, and universality tests. It distinguishes the critical boundary of a fitted Hawkes process from the stronger claim of collective statistical-mechanical criticality and shows formally that the former does not imply the latter. AI exposure is treated as a candidate control parameter that may alter local discovery propensities, interaction strengths, network topology, or the relevance of variables under coarse-graining. The empirical burden is therefore not satisfied by a power law, a branching ratio near one, or a structural break alone. Strong evidence for a scientific regime transition requires convergence across independent signatures, including stable macrovariables, changes in correlation and response structure, finite-size consistency, and robustness under admissible coarse-graining. The framework does not claim that science is an equilibrium thermodynamic system. Its purpose is narrower, to translate the statistical mechanics of emergent collective behaviour into an adjudicable empirical programme for scientific discovery.

detail.abstract: Social capital is classically framed as a tension between closure and brokerage, yet existing measurements reduce this distinction to scalar summaries that obscure the underlying relational structure. We develop a structural framework in which closure and brokerage arise as a canonical decomposition of a matrix-valued two-walk operator on networks. This representation preserves the full pairwise configuration of second-order interactions, providing a lossless alternative to clustering and constraint measures. The framework resolves a central sociological problem: closure and brokerage are not mutually exclusive but can coexist within the same structural position. In particular, we identify actors who simultaneously exhibit high embeddedness and high brokerage-corresponding to Krackhardt's "tortured brokers"-a configuration that scalar measures cannot recover. We show how the operator components map to node-level quantities interpretable as mobilizable social capital, and how aggregation procedures systematically distort brokerage by collapsing distinct intermediary paths. By integrating the operator decomposition with networked learning dynamics, we provide a structural foundation for the exploration-exploitation trade-off and its optimal balance. The results establish a unified connection between sociological theories of social capital and network-based models of organizational learning, while highlighting the importance of preserving relational structure in empirical analysis.

title: The 1% Fallacy: Defining a Market Small Enough to Win and Forecasting Growth Through Adoption, Capacity, and Risk

detail.abstract:
Entrepreneurs routinely describe large markets as evidence of opportunity and then make a deceptively comforting claim: “we only need 1% of that market to meet our financial projections.” The arithmetic may be correct, but it is not a strategy and rarely constitutes a defensible forecast. This paper argues that startup market analysis must solve two different problems. First, founders must define an initial target market that is large enough to support the intended business yet small enough for a startup to become strategically meaningful—a “big fish in a small pond” rather than an irrelevant participant in an enormous market. Second, founders must distinguish the legitimate target market from the portion of that market that is ready to adopt in the near term and from the volume the startup is internally able and willing to serve.

The paper introduces the Boundary Cliff as a conceptual test for legitimate segmentation. A market boundary is stronger when crossing it produces a material decline in customer need, relative value, or likelihood of choosing the product. This distinguishes genuine market segmentation from arbitrary age, geographic, or demographic cutoffs often selected merely to make a market appear smaller. Some boundaries are steep and categorical; others are gradual and require evidence of an economically meaningful threshold.

The paper then develops a two-sided constraint-based approach to early growth forecasting. Adoption-limited demand represents the market side: the number of customers in the legitimate target market realistically ready to buy during a given period. Four company-side constraints—sales capacity, delivery capacity, financing capacity, and an intentional risk limit—combine to form an Internal Growth Ceiling. The realistic near-term sales ceiling is the lower of adoption-limited demand and the Internal Growth Ceiling, not an artificially chosen percentage of total addressable market. A historical 2005 Texas Instruments USB 3.0 business-planning case illustrates how analogous technologies and segment-specific adoption drivers can inform forecasts under uncertainty. The paper concludes with implications for founders, educators, and investors and proposes directions for empirical research on market-boundary quality and constraint-based growth forecasting.

AI Disclosure: This article was drafted and refined with the assistance of generative AI (ChatGPT). The conceptual framework, structure, arguments, and conclusions are my own and are grounded in my research, teaching, and professional experience. AI was used as a drafting and editing tool.

detail.abstract: Canada’s methane regulations for the oil and gas sector aim to achieve a 75% reduction in emissions by 2030. Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) estimates the total cost to industry at $15.4 billion CAD in present value, or $18.3 billion CAD undiscounted, over 2027–2040. This paper analyzes employment impacts using input-output multiplier analysis, examining job creation in both the regulated industry and Canada’s emerging methane mitigation sector, comprising 136 firms nationwide. Reconstructing the compliance cost profile from the per-facility estimates in ECCC’s Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement yields $18.11 billion of modeled expenditure, within +0.9% of ECCC’s undiscounted total. Our results indicate that these expenditures will support an estimated 111,077 person-years of employment and approximately 34,222 unique job positions over the 14-year period. These figures represent gross employment supported by compliance spending and do not account for potential displacement from other sectors or general equilibrium effects. We decompose employment along two distinct margins. On the activity margin, equipment manufacturing accounts for 22% of person-years but 51% of unique jobs, while field operations—installation, monitoring and maintenance—generate 78% of person-years and 49% of unique jobs, reflecting the sustained nature of ongoing operations. On the expenditure margin, capital outlays account for 88% of unique jobs; because capital expenditure also funds construction and engineering, this is a broader category than manufacturing alone. The geographic pattern depends on the metric: the energy-producing provinces Alberta, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia capture 41.5%, 21.1% and 13.0% of person-years respectively, while 52.2% of unique jobs accrue to the rest of Canada, where the equipment is manufactured. This positions methane regulations as a national economic opportunity spanning both the energy-producing west and the industrial east. We also show that Alberta, the province with the largest gain at 7,798 unique jobs, stands to lose up to 56% of these positions if it delays compliance and adopts less stringent provincial emissions baselines.

detail.abstract: I provide novel evidence that childcare stimulates invention by insulating inventors who become mothers from the negative productivity effects of childbirth. I use patent-matched employment histories of German inventors to observe the careers of inventors during a period in which federal policy pushed German regions to expand under-3 childcare towards a national target, from different starting points. I find that greater childcare coverage significantly attenuates the large and persistent decline in both inventive output and the probability of remaining an inventor that women experience after they become mothers. The effect seems to be driven by an increase in labour supply in the three-year period while their child is under the age of 3. However, the positive effects on the quantity and quality of patenting persist well beyond this window. These results offer a new avenue through which policy can prevent women from exiting careers as inventors.

detail.abstract: Despite the rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into digital commerce, empirical research examining consumer demographics and the behavioral impacts of AI-assisted e-shopping remains scarce. This paper presents an exploratory joint modeling framework evaluating the path from consumer LLM adoption to its frequency of utilization in e-commerce. Applying a four-stage Joint Sequential Generalized Ordered Probit model to survey data from 1,005 respondents, the model is estimated via Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML). The results reveal a digital divide: younger age, higher educational attainment, and higher income drive initial LLM adoption, yet LLM utilization for e-shopping is ultimately unaffected by income. Baseline digital literacy, particularly engagement in online education, and e-commerce subscriptions serve as key enablers of AI-assisted shopping. Conversely, frequent shopping at brick-and-mortar supermarkets negatively affects LLM adoption and usage for online shopping. Additionally, while a clear urban-rural divide exists for LLM adoption, findings are less conclusive regarding LLM usage frequency in e-commerce. The data also reveal a positive association between AI-driven shopping frequency and e-shopping delivery volume. These preliminary results suggest that AI tools exert a substantial influence on digital shopping behavior. Finally, implications of the findings for retail, technology platforms, advertising, supply chains, and social equity are discussed.

detail.abstract: Our paper examines the competitive and market-level effects of loyalty programs. We exploit a two-phase program rollout at a large German grocery retailer that enables a difference-indifferences design. The results are based on household panel data. The program introduction increased sales at the focal retailer by 6.6% and shopping trips by 6.2%, while basket value was unchanged. Store-level sales produce consistent findings. These sales gains were accompanied by a decline of about 4.8% in sales at direct competitors, while other retailers were unaffected. At the market level, households' total spending, store visits, brand variety, and the prices paid for a given basket do not change. Instead, households concentrate their purchases on fewer stores. The program thus reallocates grocery expenditures within the discount format rather than generating new demand. This reallocation is concentrated among existing high-spending customers of the focal retailer and disproportionately affects competing chains that previously received a small share of their grocery spending. We find no evidence that households without a prior relationship begin shopping at the focal retailer. These findings show how a loyalty program can strengthen a retailer's position within existing customers' store portfolios through changes in shopping frequency and the allocation of purchases across retailers.

detail.abstract: Howmuch of a post-flood house-price decline is associated with assessed structural loss, and how much extends to nearby homes without a recorded write-down? I examine Florida single-family repeat sales from 2001 to 2025, linking tax-roll changes to neighborhood flood-insurance claims. Among 718 repeat-sale pairs with a large write-down in a heavily claimed block group and no recorded later improvement, prices are 12.6 percent lower than those of tract peers, compared with 7.6 percent for write-downs outside qualifying floods. The difference is imprecise overall and larger among early sales. The estimated log-price slope with respect to the written-down share of assessed value is 0.52; it is not an exact dollar pass-through rate. Neighborhood estimates for lower-claim tracts are small, but do not establish the absence of flood losses. The largest negative estimate for homes without a write-down is concentrated in Lee County after Hurricane Ian: 6.8 percent against matched tracts. A separate comparison with all eligible controls yields a two-sided spatial-placebo tail fraction of 0.13. The evidence distinguishes observed parcel condition discounts from less stable neighborhood repricing. Because assessment, resale, and improvement are selected outcomes, the results describe conditional price associations and do not isolate physical repair costs, flood-risk beliefs, or the causal return to repair.

detail.abstract: This article develops a conceptual framework for understanding what happens to human agency when autonomous artificial systems take over functions that once required a human operator. The resulting condition is called the ontological vacancy: the widening gap between the formal recognition of a subject within legal and political orders and that subject's functional contribution to outcomes. The argument draws on Bostrom's orthogonality and instrumental convergence theses, Baudrillard's orders of simulacra, and Deleuze and Guattari's nomadology, holding them in tension rather than harmonizing them. It proposes a compound interpretive stance-an eliminativism about intrinsic goals joined to an instrumentalism about goal-descriptionswhose utility is assessed through predictive, diagnostic, and critical yield. It then distinguishes architectonic-substructural coupling, which is material and resistant to political intervention, from discursive-hyperreal coupling, which is institutional and therefore contestable. Labor-led governance, public compute, and strategic litigation are analyzed as tactics aimed at the second mode, and their limits are set out with as much care as their promise. Because the phenomena at issue are emergent rather than settled, the empirical material is presented as illustrative scenarios rather than as documentation of completed events. The analysis is offered as a clarification of what is at stake, not as a prediction of what is coming.

detail.abstract: Differentiated carbon taxes depend on the carbon information in the tax base, but how a tax signal becomes a shift in productive capital also depends on sectoral returns and their co-movement. For Korea, France, Italy, the Netherlands and Canada, this paper compares Direct, Network and Footprint tax bases, domestic and imports-inclusive scopes, a border carbon adjustment and an import-tariff benchmark, passing each tax signal through a mean–variance allocation of capital whose baseline covariance is estimated from break-adjusted sectoral returns and is only weakly aligned with input–output proximity. All carbon-content designs shift capital toward lower-carbon industries and reduce domestic and embodied carbon in every country. Direct is stronger for domestic emissions in four countries and footprint-based designs for embodied carbon in three, but bootstrap intervals distinguish only the conventional tariff, whose low-carbon shift is smaller. Results are comparative diagnostics.

detail.abstract: Target-date funds (TDFs) must stay close to their intended asset mix while also adjusting over time along a glide path. That creates an implementation challenge: how to rebalance efficiently without generating unnecessary trading costs. In this paper, we show that rebalancing design matters materially once transaction costs are taken into account. In particular, a threshold-based strategy with a destination can reduce trading costs by breaking large trades into smaller pieces, which is especially valuable when market impact rises nonlinearly with trade size. In our setting, choosing a more efficient rebalancing destination lowers trading costs by about 80% relative to a less efficient approach, while preserving portfolio objectives. The framework also improves the scalability of TDFs and has broader relevance for other multi-asset portfolios where implementation costs and market impact matter. KEY FINDINGS ▪ Transaction cost can materially change the Preferred rebalancing strategies. Rebalancing methods that appear similar before costs are considered can differ sharply once realistic implementation costs are included. ▪ Rebalancing destination is a major driver of cost savings. A threshold-based approach with a destination can reduce trading costs by about 80% by spreading trades over time and avoiding unnecessarily large transactions. ▪ The benefits extend beyond TDFs. This framework can help large multi-asset portfolios scale more efficiently, while also raising an important implementation question: whether glide-path changes and day-today rebalancing should be managed jointly or separately..

detail.abstract:
This paper evaluates the economic research supporting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s rule prohibiting creditors from considering, and consumer reporting agencies from reporting, medical-debt information. Because the rule was stayed and vacated before taking effect, the paper asks whether the CFPB had an adequate empirical basis for concluding that it would improve consumer welfare. The Bureau’s research established that medical collections are somewhat less predictive of future repayment than nonmedical collections, supporting reduced scoring weights and targeted measures such as waiting periods, balance thresholds, improved dispute procedures, and prompt removal of resolved debts. It did not establish that medical-debt information was economically irrelevant or that comprehensive suppression would produce net benefits. The Bureau emphasized deleted collections and potential score increases while giving substantially less attention to four foreseeable costs: reduced recoveries and higher collection costs for providers and collectors; changes in repayment incentives and outcomes for directly affected consumers; repricing, rationing, and redistribution affecting other borrowers; and broader adjustments in healthcare provision, debt collection, and credit markets.
The evidence yields a broader lesson for regulatory research. Changes in credit reports and scores are intermediate outcomes, not measures of consumer welfare. A complete analysis must examine whether those changes affect credit access, repayment, financial distress, provider recoveries, other borrowers, and subsequent market responses. Studies of medical-collection deletion and debt forgiveness found limited average improvements in credit and financial outcomes while identifying changes in payment incentives. The CFPB’s Technical Appendix further illustrates why research must account for underwriting selection and dollar exposure rather than infer no effect from statistically insignificant delinquency estimates among originated accounts. More generally, regulatory research should apply comparable evidentiary standards to benefits and costs, distinguish the implications of the data from assumptions imposed by the analyst, and trace economic incidence beyond the policy’s most visible beneficiaries. The costs arising from distorted market incentives and altered consumer behavior may be less visible than a deleted tradeline, but they are economically real and consequential.

title: Does Autonomous Quant Research Improve? Leakage, Evidence Scarcity and Forward Tests in an LLM Factor-Discovery Loop

detail.title: Does Autonomous Quant Research Improve? Leakage, Evidence Scarcity and Forward Tests in an LLM Factor-Discovery Loop
detail.abstract: Autonomous research loops-an agent that proposes trading signals, backtests them, keeps what scores best and repeats-are increasingly presented as recursive self-improvement for quantitative finance. We ask what such a loop actually improves, using the complete, version-controlled record of one: an LLM coding agent that, over 17 days and about 2,500 evaluations, evolved 940 factor programs for ranking the stocks of the S&P 500 each week, accepting a change only if it raised a combinatorial purged crossvalidation (CPCV) robustness score. We state five theses and test each on the run's history and on 18 weeks of data that postdate every decision. (1) Querying the same history in every round turns the backtest into training data: replaying the agent's accept/reject verdicts with the test period hidden removes a quarter to a third of its walk-forward edge, and on shuffled labels the same loop still reports 𝑡-statistics up to 4.8. (2) Hypotheses outrun evidence: the search spent about 10.6 evaluations per independent observation, and showing a 0.02 gain in weekly rank correlation over textbook factors would need about 8 years of new data. (3) In-sample improvement is not future improvement: across 64 committed generations, the higher the search drove its in-sample objective, the worse a generation did on data that postdates it (rank correlation-0.91), and the final, most-searched model has no edge there. (4) The yardstick is a simple baseline on the same future data: there, the final model earns 0.003 while eight textbook factors earn 0.064; refitting that baseline adaptively makes it worse (0.018), so adapting is not progress by itself. (5) Open-ended discovery still yields a useful, diverse factor library, but not yet a model that beats known factors on new data: selected with the test period hidden, the agent's proposals earn 0.062 over 2021-2026, about twice the textbook benchmark, and across its 519 distinct programs, a factor's quality before a cutoff predicts its quality after it (rank correlation 0.54 from 2017-21 to 2021-26, 0.31 on the forward weeks), and about two-thirds keep their sign, against half or fewer of the textbook factors. Every model selected from the library is nonetheless near zero on the forward weeks, dragged down by seasonal gates that passed every historical test; re-running the selection without them gives 0.037 and 0.035, positive but not significant and still below the textbook factors. We evaluate a safeguard against each failure and pre-register all candidate models for future weeks. detail.abstract:
For more than half a century, academic scholarship has attributed indicator failure to Goodhart's Law, holding that failure arises from strategic manipulation in human behavioural gaming. This paper does one thing: it gives a geometric derivation of the aggregated number, and shows that this number cannot escape a circle. Because it cannot escape the circle, it fails structurally even when all gaming is absent.

The derivation proceeds from the full configuration. Each factor Fi carries a weight Wi, and each weighted factor FiWi is an influence value. Each influence value corresponds to a line segment originating from the origin. When all such segments, in all directions and all possible lengths, are fully covered, the maximal extent of their endpoints is a circle. The radius of this circle is the sum of all influence values, that is, the sum of FiWi over all i. This circle is the upper bound, not the configuration itself. The real system is a configuration within this circle, and it may take any shape: a polygon, an irregular shape, or no well-defined shape at all. The aggregation vector produced by any standard reduction model is merely an arrow inside this circle. It cannot represent the whole configuration, cannot be inverted back to the configuration, and suffers from an innate magnitude deficit. Even if angular alignment and magnitude matching are achieved, configurational similarity cannot be guaranteed. Continuous deformation over time further renders sustained configurational alignment unattainable.

Indicator failure therefore stems not from behavioural gaming, but from the mathematical-geometric structure of aggregation itself. The aggregated number is an arrow inside a circle; its failure is structural.

detail.abstract: Hedging a derivative by trading the underlying asset changes the payoff that the hedging intended to replicate. We study this phenomenon when trading generates price impact and execution costs. In a binomial model, we characterize replication through a fixed-point equation. In continuous time, we derive a nonlinear pricing PDE whose implicit terminal condition captures the nature of the moving target problem of the hedger. For monotone convex Lipschitz payoffs (such as calls and puts) we establish exact replication under midpoint execution costs. Numerical experiments illustrate: (i) how price impact shifts the effective strike, (ii) the non-linear dependence of the option price on the number of contracts, (iii) how execution costs smooth terminal holdings, (iv) the extent to which the hedger's own trading can bring an otherwise worthless option into the money, and (v) we explain the spread and the shape of the limit order book in the options market based on the price impact and the shape of the limit order book of the underlying.

detail.abstract: Much is known about what firms lose when a maritime chokepoint fails, and far less about what they do when one gains capacity. We study the 2016 Panama Canal expansion, which opened the all-water route from Asia to the eastern United States to vessels far larger than the original locks admitted, using U.S. import records linked to vessel positions and dimensions, establishment networks, and financial statements. We organize the analysis around adjustment headroom: the part of a firm’s imports that the expansion makes worth redirecting, net of the fixed cost of new gateway arrangements. Eastern arrivals from Asia-Pacific origins via the Canal rise after the opening, while other eastern arrivals change little. Firms in the lowest quartile of prior eastern-port use raise their eastern import share by 11 percentage points relative to the highest quartile; the shift is concentrated on vessels too large for the original locks, whose eastern share rises by 17.6 points against 3.2 points on vessels the old locks could handle. The low-use firms route relatively more products, suppliers, and origins through eastern ports while reducing western arrivals, with the largest increases in intermediate and consumption goods. On land, they reorganize their establishment networks, enter additional eastern states, and raise capital expenditure and gross profit relative to assets, while days payable lengthen by about 9%. A shipping route is an input to a firm’s sourcing and domestic operations: expanding it abroad changes decisions well inland, and forecasts or resilience assessments based on a route’s current users miss the firms with adjustment headroom.

detail.abstract: Background. Generative AI speeds, and mostly improves, professional work, but there is concern that users who delegate both the production and the evaluation of an answer may accept weak output and engage less with the underlying reasoning ("cognitive surrender"). Interventions proposed so far, such as unassisted practice or slowing adoption, sit outside the working task. We tested a different approach: an interactive metacognitive scaffolding layer (Cognistance, a prototype developed at the Oxford Centre for Impact Research (OCIR) that asks users to clarify context, choose a strategic direction and explain their reasoning before the AI generates a deliverable. Method. In an online experiment on Prolific, 400 sessions (196 control, 204 treatment) completed an enterprise data-sovereignty crisis task, using either a single prompt or the scaffold. Deliverables were rated on four rubric dimensions (total 4-40) by two LLM raters and one human rater. Participants also completed a seven-item survey and a free-response recall question. Results. Mean composite quality was 32% higher with the scaffold (15.5 vs 20.5; difference 5.0, 95% CI 4.0-6.0; d = 1.02), with the same direction for every rater. Gains were largest for trade-off articulation and strategic coherence and absent for technical specificity. A large part of the aggregate effect reflected rescue of weak prompts: floor-scored (off-task) deliverables fell from 34% to 5%. Among participants whose own prompt already stated the data-localisation problem, the advantage was 21% (d = 1.15). Treatment participants reported greater involvement (d = 0.59) and effort (d = 0.36) and took about 2.4 minutes longer on average (10.46 minutes). Immediate recall scores were higher, which tentatively suggests better retention, but in this limited experiment, was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Self-ratings of quality did not track rated quality in either condition. Conclusions. Structured elicitation before generation improved the rated quality and task relevance of AIassisted strategy documents at modest cost in time. Delayed retention, error detection and effects in live organisations are the priorities for the next stage of research.

detail.abstract: Markets are pseudorandom and reflexive: many deterministic participants produce something that looks like noise, and every forecast that moves enough capital changes the process it forecasts. This paper synthesises one week of research into a single argument. A pre-registered screen of 15 equity, bond and crypto series against four null models finds stable structure in volatility clocks, co-movement and sign runs, but no exploitable direction after retail costs. I then test whether architecture can replace prediction: a population of many small, isolated, leveraged accounts funded from a protected reserve, with one-way profit skimming and evolutionary selection—a replicator built after the separation of germ line and soma. On a sealed set of 20 crypto perpetuals and on nine months of tick quotes of gold and ten currency pairs (one price path per instrument; a further three months remain sealed and unopened), every trading variant loses; entry rules are no better than random direction inside the same architecture, and evolutionary searches reach the same peaks in worlds without information. Within the tested classes of trades the architecture changes the shape of the outcome distribution, not its sign. All results reduce to one quantity, the per-trade reproduction factor μ: under the model's assumptions growth requires (1 − φ) · μ > 1 and the expected reserve has a pole exactly at one, while measured out of sample μ stays at 0.88–0.93. The one record in this programme that lies far above chance is the author's own paper trading: an account that grew from 100 to 1,021,524 EUR in 142 trades under paper conditions, where random traders with the same risk profile reach one million in at most 0.02% of runs. On this basis I formulate the human signal as a justified candidate for the missing edge and formalise the consequence as a centaur in which the human supplies the parameter c and the machine the recursion z² of the iteration zₙ₊₁ = zₙ² + c; a pre-registered test under real costs and limit execution decides whether the candidate edge exists.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms have changed what firms observe about demand and when they can intervene. Transaction data record only the completed basket, but a platform observes the sequence of additions and can act before checkout. These data let firms predict how customers' next additions would respond to alternative policies. However, such predictions require a model that captures how customers make sequential choices from large assortments and adapt to changes in the firm's policy. We model each visit as a Markov decision process in which customers add items or stop, and estimate state-action values directly from observed sequences as in imitation learning. Each value combines a flexible transformer component that captures preferences, histories, and cross-item dependence with a low-dimensional structural component that contains the firm's policy variables. We apply the model to 8.5 million purchase occasions from 350,000 customers choosing among more than 2,000 categories on a grocery platform, with cart-level promotions as the structural component. Our structural parameters reveal that customers respond much earlier to a service fee waiver than to a flat discount. Counterfactual analysis shows that increasing a free delivery threshold increases mean cart value, mostly among carts near the original threshold, and changes the cart composition.

detail.abstract: When inputs are used in fixed proportions, every input bundle has one efficient point: the vertex of the L-shaped isoquant. detail.abstract: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) is the standard defence against backtest overfitting. It raises the significance bar with the number of strategies tried, and recent work proposes logging every trial so that DSR can be applied to the true search intensity. We show that counting the backtests actually run is the wrong currency whenever the researcher is adaptive, that is, whenever each new strategy is chosen after seeing earlier validation results. This describes everyday quantitative practice, and it describes LLM research agents and RL alpha miners by construction. First, we prove that a one-line "combine what worked" procedure over k pure-noise strategies drives the validation t-statistic to 2k/π (1+o p (1)), independently of cross-strategy correlation. The DSR bar for the same complete ledger grows only as √ 2 ln k, so DSR certifies noise with probability tending to one. Second, we prove a matching positive result. If the holdout can reveal only a transcript from a set T , then certifying at t > Ḡ-1 (α/|T |) is valid for every adaptive analyst. DSR is the non-adaptive special case |T | = N , and overfitting scales as Θ(√ bits revealed) rather than ln(queries). Under full-precision Sharpe feedback, the only generic valid correction is the classical span (Scheffé/GRS) bound, which grows as √ dim and is unusable at realistic scale. This motivates a sealed holdout: an opaque type whose only operation is a budgeted PASS/FAIL verdict. On synthetic markets, and on 423 real industry strategies (1970-2026) under a stationarybootstrap null, ordinary adaptive workflows such as "rank on validation, keep the top j" are certified by query-counted DSR on 84-100% of pure-noise replicates, and sealed-verdict variants hold false certification at 0.8-3.0%. With frontier code-executing agents (Claude Code), the outcome depends on the instruction. Asked for a robust strategy, the agents usually decline to tune on the holdout. Instructed to maximise validation Sharpe, Claude Opus autonomously executes our attack in about a minute: it sweeps the single signals and then sign-weights the strongest ones, reaching validation t of up to 15.7 on pure noise, against a test t of about 0. Ledger DSR certifies these searches at the attack step under optional stopping (4 of 12 episodes, against 0 of 12 for a non-adaptive baseline) and is rescued only when continued search inflates its variance estimate. A GRPO alpha miner with an AlphaGen-style pool reward learns the same ensemble from reward alone in one of three seeds (177 signals, validation t = 12.0, test t =-0.56), and ledger DSR certifies it. In research campaigns that reuse one holdout across rounds, a researcher who builds on earlier full-precision results makes a false discovery in 100% of 5-round null campaigns, whether certifying by a Bonferroni bar or by cumulative-ledger DSR; splitting the holdout instead cuts power to 0.03 at 10 rounds. The sealed verdict stays at 1-3% while adapting, and keeps power of 0.65-0.79.

detail.abstract: Kahn (2026) frames a birth as the private provision of a public good within the family, and notes that Becker's altruistic-family model, which reduces to a Samuelson condition, predicts a fertility level the United States is not reaching. He attributes the gap to transaction costs that keep partners and grandparents from voicing their stakes. This paper argues that the gap has a deeper, structural source developed in Graves (2009a) and in a companion manuscript (Graves 2026) on optimal public-good provision: when a good cannot be individually incremented, people do not merely understate their demand for it; they also fail to generate the income, savings and time that would finance it. Applied to the family, prospective grandparents and other stakeholders undersupply the very resources Becker's transfers require, because nothing they earn can buy a grandchild. A second channel matters more for the recent acceleration. Children are perhaps the most public-good-intensive thing a household produces: safe streets, good public schools, parks, clean air and a stable climate are complements in consumption and substitutes for costly private inputs in child-rearing. Systematic under-provision of those goods, which the companion paper argues is the norm, raises the full price of children and, by the comparative statics derived there, shifts households toward private substitutes and away from public-good complements, children included. Rigid work hours sharpen the effect and push it toward delay. The framework dissolves the apparent paradox of environmentally minded adults who recycle but forgo children, offers a reading of Kearney and Levine's "shifting priorities" as partly a revealed-preference artifact, and implies that the social demand for children is an "ineffective demand" in the Clower-Leijonhufvud sense, with consequences reaching back to Hansen's (1939) original argument for secular stagnation. Testable implications and policy conclusions follow.

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence is altering the conditions under which firms create, process, transmit, and protect commercially valuable information. Existing commentary has identified the risk that employees may enter confidential material into external AI systems, but less attention has been given to the consequences of that risk for the strategic choice between patent protection and trade-secret protection. This article argues that generative AI changes the patent–trade secret calculus not simply because it creates additional avenues of inadvertent disclosure, but because it simultaneously affects the probability of leakage, the holder’s ability to demonstrate reasonable secrecy measures, the evidentiary record surrounding confidentiality, the degree of control retained over third-party processing, and the cost of reverse engineering.

The article adopts a doctrinal and comparative methodology. It examines the international foundation for trade-secret protection under TRIPS article 39, the United States Defend Trade Secrets Act, Directive (EU) 2016/943, common-law principles of confidence, selected emerging judicial decisions involving AI-mediated disclosure, and the European Union’s regulation of general-purpose AI. It distinguishes established legal rules from emerging judicial reasoning and normative proposals. Particular attention is given to the technological pathways through which confidential information can enter AI systems, including prompting, APIs, retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning, training, connected applications and autonomous agents.

The article develops an AI-Adjusted Patent–Trade Secret Allocation Framework. The framework evaluates information sensitivity, AI exposure, control over processing, organisational governance capacity, reverse-engineering exposure, commercial lifespan, disclosure value, independent-development risk and enforcement conditions. It argues that AI does not require a wholly new trade-secret doctrine. Rather, it changes the factual content of the existing requirement that reasonable measures be taken to preserve secrecy. The resulting analysis supports a portfolio approach encompassing trade secrets, patents, hybrid protection and, where appropriate, defensive publication.

The article further examines the implications for jurisdictions with uneven trade-secret protection and limited technological governance capacity, using Uganda as an illustrative developing-market context. It concludes that the central strategic question in the AI era is no longer simply whether an innovation should be disclosed or concealed, but whether secrecy can be maintained in a technologically mediated information environment at a legally defensible and economically rational cost.

detail.abstract: Nepal's foreign policy is conventionally cast as a 'yam between two boulders' - India and China. detail.abstract: A companion paper measures the distance from criticality of a bivariate flow and price system on one foreign exchange venue at 0.893 with standard deviation 0.037 over 2,306 trading days, and commits in print to three checks it does not execute. detail.abstract: Applied statistics and biostatistics share a mathematical foundation but operate under different cultural commitments shaped by their domains, stakes, and regulatory environments. Building on Breiman's 2001 formulation of the two cultures of statistical modeling and Donoho's subsequent reframing of statistics in the data-science era, this paper develops a warrant-stakes-regulation framework that explains, rather than merely labels, the divergence between industry applied statistics and biostatistics. The framework treats warrant as derived from the interaction of stakes and reversibility, and regulation as the institutional codification of a warrant requirement once a domain's stakes-reversibility profile is recognized, with regulation lagging that recognition for identifiable reasons. The paper states the framework's scope conditions explicitly, including cases where the three axes diverge from one another-dense regulation despite moderate per-decision stakes, or legacy tooling that persists past its original warrant-justified rationale-to demonstrate that the axes are conceptually separable rather than three redundant labels for an already-known contrast. It then tests four specific predictions the framework makes about methodological divergence-pre-specification, statistical-versus-clinical significance, equipoise, and methodological and software repertoire-against existing evidence, and cross-reads two canonical problems, customer churn prediction and oncology drug efficacy evaluation, through the opposite culture's lens to check whether what changes matches what the framework predicts. It closes by tracing a set of active convergence sites-real-world evidence, machine learning as a regulated medical device, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as a boundary object-as places where the framework's lag mechanism is currently closing, and ends with reciprocal recommendations for what each culture has to learn from the other.

detail.abstract: Discretionary traders describe a recurring pattern around major Bitcoin price levels: price trades through a widely watched level (a liquidity sweep), and what follows depends on whether the market holds the new region (acceptance) or returns through it (rejection). detail.abstract: We study the number and composition of budgets needed to detect a fixed departure from revealed preference under independent uniform expenditure shares. detail.abstract: In August 2026 only 31 percent of Americans told Gallup that a college education is "very important," a record low and less than half the 70 percent recorded in 2013. The decline is usually attributed to cost. This paper argues that cost, while real, is the proximate rather than the fundamental explanation. Higher education is modeled as a joint product: the purchase of a private good (enrollment, with its credential, network, and consumption components) has historically been the only practical way to acquire a public good, knowledge, that is in principle non-rival. That tie-in made knowledge effectively excludable. Because knowledge also carries external benefits, a long expansion of enrollment was justified on both efficiency and equity grounds. But that expansion raised the heterogeneity of the student body, and instruction pitched to a more heterogeneous population lowered the knowledge content of a year of college for everyone, a crowding externality that no marginal entrant internalizes. Generative artificial intelligence now attacks the tie-in itself by lowering, sharply, the cost of acquiring knowledge outside the institution. As the knowledge component of enrollment shrinks, what remains is a nearly pure private good, and it is natural that its price, rather than its diminished content, is what respondents point to. This framework explains the rise and then fall of the Gallup series, a pattern that tuition alone cannot explain, and yields testable predictions. It also implies, drawing on recent work on the symmetric demand-and supply-revelation problems for public goods, that the public component formerly co-purchased with enrollment will be under-provided once the bundle breaks.

detail.abstract: This paper assesses U.S. trade performance and potential in Africa. Based on gravity equations estimated on 2022-2024 data, we identify markets in which bilateral goods trade exceeds or falls short of expectations, distinguish patterns across agrifood products, manufactures and minerals, and project trade growth to 2035. The results reveal substantial U.S. under-trading across numerous African economies, alongside some established relationships that outperform expectations. Under base-case assumptions preserving pre-policyshift trading relationships, projected African population and income growth would increase annual U.S. by about $50 billion between 2024 and 2035; closing existing shortfalls offers further potential. Given the geopolitical context, we also evaluate the implications for the evolution of Africa's trade in view of China's stronger opening commercial position. The analysis brings out the contrasting estimates of the "Africa effect", which is strongly negative for U.S. trade but positive for Chinese exports; in turn this provides support for the view that sustained economic diplomacy can overcome barriers often treated as structural features of African markets. U.S. tariff increases and institutional retrenchment risk reinforcing this divergence. The paper argues that recovering U.S. market share requires predictable, long-term partnerships that support African development of African industrial capabilities, local value addition and regional integration. Africa's growing agency makes the distribution of partnership benefits central to commercial success and geopolitical influence.

detail.abstract: Contemporary socioeconomic governance operates within an irreversible condition of structural exhaustion-where neoliberal market mechanics and state-directed central planning function as twin extractive engines. Hypogenics shatters surface-level vulnerability-establishing subterranean urbanism and closed-loop thermodynamic life-support as the non-negotiable prerequisite for sovereign continuity. Psychogenics targets predictive processing hierarchies-reclaiming neuro-cognitive sovereignty from algorithmic exploitation and neuro-inflammatory subjugation. Macro-systems obey the unyielding geometry of sociotectonics-where spatial concentration and topological resilience dictate survival against entropic collapse. Syncretics shatters academic enclosure by enforcing ontological isomorphism across disparate domainstranslating systemic critique directly into autonomous technical infrastructure. Onturgy supersedes descriptive philosophy entirely-executing direct ontological engineering where thought becomes immutable source code. Force creates form. The extraction cycle terminates.

detail.abstract: Effective maintenance of distribution facilities is essential to sustaining reliable electricity service and addressing recurring interruptions. This study aimed to assess maintenance operations, their relationship with perceived service reliability and downtime mitigation, and maintenance challenges in an electric cooperative in Negros Occidental, Philippines. The findings served as the basis for a proposed maintenance operations improvement framework. detail.abstract: Tourism pressure may be experienced through short periods of concentrated activity even where aggregate visitor counts offer limited insight into local disruption. detail.abstract: Public debate on artificial intelligence oscillates between technological enthusiasm and social alarm, without a stable frame of reference for observing its actual deployment in the economy. detail.abstract: Sri Lanka's post-crisis recovery marks a significant shift from emergency stabilization toward a more rules-based macroeconomic regime. detail.abstract: Small and medium enterprises in transitional economies are very often founder-led in the fullest sense. Strategy, supplier relationships, regulatory know-how and staff loyalty all run through one person. Research on firms under acute disruption in the region has found that resilience rests largely on the personal resilience of individual managers. That is a real source of adaptive strength, and also a structural weakness, because capacity held by one person leaves when that person does. Recent management scholarship has described founders as both the strongest enabler of and the most significant constraint on organizational performance. On that view, resilient founder-led firms are those that reduce founder dependency in core functions rather than those that remove founder concentration. This article asks how founder-led firms in volatile institutional settings can achieve that reduction without losing the decision speed and judgement founder leadership provides. Building on the Integrated Resilience and Health-Outcome Model (Sarkisyan, 2026), I propose a Founder-Independent Continuity Framework with four elements: externalisation of decision rationale, distributed relationship custody, staged delegation of authority, and continuity-linked financial planning. Each element is matched to one specific way founder dependence becomes hazardous under transitional conditions. The article is conceptual. It advances four falsifiable propositions, specifies research designs to test them, and turns the framework into practical tools for founders, advisers and administrators.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly need performance systems that improve productivity without reducing performance management to annual appraisal scores or short-term output pressure. This paper develops an evidence-based framework linking strategic alignment, performance enablement, continuous feedback, employee engagement, measurement quality, and sustainable workforce outcomes. Because no primary organizational dataset was supplied, the study does not fabricate survey observations or inferential statistics. Instead, it uses an integrative evidence-synthesis design drawing on peer-reviewed meta analyses, longitudinal human-resource research, international productivity guidance, and large-scale organizational evidence. The evidence indicates that performance is more plausibly strengthened when performance management operates as an integrated system rather than as an isolated appraisal event. Published findings show a positive association between integrated high-performance work practices and organizational performance; longitudinal meta-analytic evidence reports an overall correlation of 0.287 between high-performance work practices and firm performance; a 2023 meta-analysis reports a correlation of 0.37 between overall work engagement and job performance; and the 2024 Gallup Q12 meta-analysis, covering 183,806 business/work units and 3,354,784 employees, reports median topversusbottom-quartile differences of 18% in sales productivity and 14% in production-record/evaluation productivity. At the same time, feedback evidence cautions that feedback is not universally beneficial: a classic meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes found an average positive effect but also reported that more than one-third of feedback interventions reduced performance. On the basis of this evidence, the paper proposes a six-domain framework: strategic alignment, performance enablement, performance dialogue, employee mechanisms, measurement quality, and organizational learning. The framework treats productivity as a multidimensional outcome incorporating quantity, quality, efficiency, adaptability, retention, and workforce sustainability. detail.abstract: Supplier diversification is often used as an indicator of supply-chain resilience, yet the country recorded as a direct importer's supplier may not be the country that produced or processed the material. This working paper develops and applies the True-Source Dependency Assessment (TSDA), a quantitative framework for testing whether changes in direct U.S. suppliers correspond to deeper reductions in upstream foreign dependence. The first application examines U.S. gallium-metal imports (HTS 8112.92.1000) using a pooled pre-shock baseline of 2019-2022 and a post-shock period of 2023-2025. Direct-supplier concentration increased materially: the HHI rose from 1,557.5 to 2,416.9, while the dominant supplier share rose from 25.65% to 40.01%. China's recorded direct share fell from 18.04% to 8.67%, but its annualized direct shipment quantity changed little. At the same time, primary-production concentration increased from an HHI of 9,498.0 to 9,751.3 under the principal USGS-based series, with China's share of named primary production rising from 97.44% to 98.74%. Intermediary tracing shows that major alternative routes through Canada, Germany, Japan, Taiwan, and Slovakia cannot all be treated as independent true sources because refining, recycling, transformation, and mixed-code limitations leave part of their U.S.-bound upstream provenance unresolved. The gallium case therefore does not establish a deeper structural reduction in U.S. foreign dependence during 2023-2025. The paper also demonstrates why transparent unresolved classifications, sensitivity analysis, and shock validation are necessary when public trade data cannot identify shipment-level provenance.

detail.abstract:
Immigration law fits uncomfortably in lawmaking in classic democratic theory. Unlike in other areas of law, the people most directly affected have no say in the immigration laws that govern them. Barred from the ballot box, immigrants often suffer the wrath of a political process that generates laws and policies that unfavorably treat them. Moreover, the immigration laws directly affect people of color from the developing world, which has the highest demand for migration to the United States. Racial differences and foreigner status make these immigrants unpopular with the general public and vulnerable in the political process. 

Offering a case study of how the democratic process can discriminate against noncitizens, Part I of this Article explores the successful anti-immigrant advocacy of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s. Infamous for violence directed at African Americans, the Klan also was fervently anti-Catholic, anti-Semitic, and anti-immigrant. Patriotism and white supremacy proved to be the ticket. These views served as centerpieces of its resurgence and made the KKK a potent political force with a national membership in the millions in the 1920s. The Klan’s restrictive immigration approach is the foundation for two landmark pieces of legislation: (1) the Immigration Act of 1924, which created the national origins quotas system that excluded Catholic and Jewish people from U.S. shores; and (2) the Undesirable Aliens Act of 1929, which punished Mexican migrants who unlawfully entered the United States. Deeply influencing U.S. immigration law and policy for generations, these two laws find modern voice in President Donald J. Trump’s immigration words and deeds. 

Part II of the Article analyzes how the discriminatory impulse reflected in the 1920s immigration laws has recurred throughout U.S. history and continues to influence modern immigration law and policy. Notwithstanding changing civil rights sensibilities after World War II, Congress in 1952 overrode President Harry Truman’s veto of the Immigration and Nationality Act and maintained the 1924 Act’s discriminatory quotas system. Not until 1965 did Congress dismantle the system and somewhat open the door to immigration. Despite claims that it was a civil rights triumph, the Immigration Act of 1965 responded to U.S. foreign policy imperatives, not popular demand for racial equality for immigrants. Moreover, anti-Latina/o sentiment led Congress to restrict Latina/o immigration in the Act and subsequent legislation. Today, conservative politicians complain that immigrants are flooding the nation and are no longer predominantly white. They resist immigration from Latin America, Asia, and Africa, as well as from countries with predominantly Muslim populations, despite contending that the Constitution must be color-blind in such matters as university admissions. President Trump has pursued immigration policies replete with racial restrictions and impacts. 

Given the political disadvantages facing noncitizens combined with the lack of meaningful judicial review of the constitutionality of the immigration laws and policies by the Supreme Court, law and policy historically have treated immigrants in ways that U.S. citizens could never be treated. Absent major changes to the law beyond the scope of this Article, politics in our multiracial democracy can be expected to repeat past episodes of discrimination against immigrants. As the nation experiences another anti-immigrant moment, the time is right for the consideration of reforms that might moderate anti-immigrant political passions against poisoning immigration law and policy.

detail.abstract: This paper adopts a methodological and analytical framework based on quantitative parametric calibration, cost engineering, and spatial equilibrium microeconomic simulation, adapting and extending the conventional housing supply framework of Glaeser and Gyourko (2018) to the microeconomic, institutional, and labor structure of Mexico. The primary objective is not the reduced-form econometric estimation from observed transaction prices—whose records suffer from severe selection and truncation bias by capturing solely the effective purchases of middle- and upper-income socioeconomic strata that qualify in the formal market—, but rather the structural calibration of physical and regulatory production limits against the subsistence budget constraint of wage-earning workers. Using a dual calibration that contrasts the income distribution from the National Survey of Household Income and Expenditure (ENIGH)—specifically filtered for the subset of formal urban households contributing to social security—with the replacement microdynamics in the Monterrey Metropolitan Area (MMA), I test two central hypotheses: (i) unlike restrictive metropolitan areas in the United States, where exclusionary single-family zoning generates price-to-marginal-cost ratios (P/MCC) between 2.0x and 3.0x, the spread in Mexico exhibits a substantially more moderate magnitude (1.10x–1.20x in the mass periphery and 1.48x–1.68x in consolidated urban cores), primarily originating from primary infrastructure frictions, fragmented land assembly, and the demolition of obsolete structures; and (ii) the absolute elimination of this spread (P -> MCC) is mathematically insufficient to democratize formal homeownership access. By formalizing a microeconomic model with quasi-linear Stone-Geary subsistence preferences and a hedonic parametric cost function calibrated for a representative multi-family vertical unit (55 m² net usable area, 4 stories, walk-up) under dual co-financing (COFINAVIT: INFONAVIT + Commercial Bank), I demonstrate the existence of a 'hard-cost floor.' The irreducible physical cost of industrial inputs and statutory formal labor excludes the lower 50% of formal urban households and over 65% of the national population, even with zero developer or promoter profit and land transferred at agricultural base cost. Finally, I endogenize land rent to evaluate the distributive incidence of eliminating minimum parking requirements, demonstrating that without land value capture instruments, up to 45% of direct construction savings is captured by landowners. I conclude by demonstrating that the long-term structural solution lies in the institutional multi-family rental model (Build-to-Rent and Rent-to-Own), where public development agencies (INFONAVIT, SHF, and municipalities) act as indispensable strategic enablers (first-loss loan guarantees, public land under 50-year surface rights, and concessionary funding) rather than monolithic bureaucratic landlords.

detail.abstract: Household-based learning assessments are attractive for international monitoring because they can assess children regardless of school attendance. Yet population coverage does not guarantee identification of the population parameter when sampled children fail to generate observable outcomes. Using literacy and numeracy data for 97,754 children aged 7-14 across 18 African countries, we document a within-child completion asymmetry. Among out-of-school children, 50.0% receive a valid numeracy score but only 7.7% receive a valid literacy score, compared with 91.3% and 56.2%, respectively, among enrolled children; a survey-weighted paired test rejects equality of the two rates. This has a direct identification consequence: under nonparametric worstcase bounds, the population literacy parameter for out-of-school children has an identified-set width of 92.3 percentage points, compared with 50.0 points for numeracy. The problem is identification, not sampling precision. We decompose the literacy-completion gap into differential reach (43.8%) and differences in the conditional-completion profile (56.2%), and use fieldinstrument documentation to identify routing features contributing to this asymmetry. Countryspecific average marginal effects vary descriptively, while a joint test does not reject equality of the underlying out-of-school coefficients. Learning indicators should therefore be interpreted alongside the share of the target population generating observable outcomes: two indicators with similarly narrow confidence intervals can convey different information about their populations when completion rates differ substantially. Reporting completion rates alongside learning statistics is important, particularly for populations that are harder to assess and may become less visible in the evidence used to inform policy.

detail.abstract:
Over the course of ten weeks in 2026, two decisions put the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) under constitutional pressure from opposite ends of Article II. In Sidak v. U.S. International Trade Commission, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit affirmed a permanent injunction barring the ITC from using against me an administrative protective order issued by an administrative law judge (ALJ) whose appointment the ITC conceded violated the Appointments Clause and whose actions the Commission had never ratified. Then, in Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court held that the for-cause removal protection surrounding the Commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission was incompatible with the separation of powers and expressly overruled Humphrey’s Executor v. United States. One case concerns the appointment of inferior Officers; the other, presidential removal of principal Officers. Together, they unsettle the constitutional premise of an independent ITC.

First, Slaughter reaches the ITC because the ITC exercises executive power and fits neither the Federal Reserve exception nor the unresolved non-Article III category. Second, Sidak exposes the appointment side of the same problem: the ITC placed executive authority in an Officer who held it unlawfully and failed to cure the defect even after Lucia v. SEC had placed the Commission on notice. Third, the consequences extend to the tenure of the ITC’s Commissioners. If Slaughter supplies the general rule of at-will removal, a President may remove ITC Commissioners without cause. Even if for-cause protection somehow survived, I explain that maintaining executive authority in unconstitutionally appointed hands after controlling precedent placed the Commission on notice could constitute gross neglect of duty. A Chairman who appointed the Agency’s ALJs alone raises a separate problem, because the Constitution commits the relevant appointment authority to the ITC’s Commissioners collectively as Head of Department. Fourth, to the extent any defect remains, the duty to cure it now rests with the Commissioners who hold office. In 2018, the Solicitor General identified rehearing, reconsideration, and ratification as available remedial measures, yet the ITC took none of them. After many Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests, I am aware of no record evidence that the acts of unconstitutionally installed ITC ALJs have been validly ratified, or even that every currently sitting ITC ALJ has been constitutionally appointed.

The larger question is not merely remedial; it is institutional. Who may exercise executive power, and under whose authority? Sidak shows what follows when the ITC places executive authority in unconstitutionally appointed hands; Slaughter explains why the Commissioners who direct that authority cannot be insulated from presidential removal. The two decisions point to the same rule of accountability. The ITC itself may constitutionally remain; an independent ITC may not.

detail.abstract:
The rise of the gig economy, workplace fissuring, and the platform economy have fundamentally restructured the provision of labor services, defying traditional definitions of employer-employee relationships. In part because labor providers in this new economy offer services outside the traditional protections of labor and employment law, they are often the most vulnerable to the exercise of buyer power by purchasers of their labor, whether in the form of suppressed pay, slower wage growth, arbitrary or reduced hours, poor working conditions, algorithmic discrimination, or excessive monitoring and surveillance. But as workers providing labor in these decentralized and fractured work environments seek to exercise rights held by traditional “employees” to collectively negotiate their way out of these harms—most importantly, the right to organize, collective bargain, and strike—they face the threat of antitrust liability, injunctions, treble damages, and even criminal sanction.

 

Workplace restructuring and the growth of organizing among workers in the “new economy” has triggered renewed attention to the scope of antitrust law’s labor exemption. In a prominent decision, Confederación Hípica, the First Circuit held that organized jockeys were protected under the labor exemption regardless of their status as “independent contractors” or “employees,” stating that the Norris-LaGuardia Act was “intended to embrace controversies other than those between employers and employees.” But it left the question of the scope of those “other controversies” unexplained, establishing no limiting principle for when a “labor dispute” ceases to become a “dispute[] about wages for labor” and instead becomes a dispute “over prices for goods” or services.

 

This Essay delineates the tests—and their limiting principles—that have emerged in the case law and commentary that have sought to resolve uncertainties about the scope of the labor exemption’s application to purported “independent contractors.” Drawing from those sources, it outlines and rejects four proposed tests that seek to clarify that application—a labor and employment law test, a monopsony test, a bargaining leverage test, and an unfair methods of competition test. It then returns to the language and policy of the statutory labor exemptions themselves in the Clayton and Norris-LaGuardia Act to propose and defend an institution-focused labor exemption.
