detail.abstract:
This paper uses a second method to test the hypothesis that the composition of household wealth moderates the transmission of monetary policy to consumption: a dollar of revaluation in equities would move less spending than a dollar of revaluation in housing. It follows the design of Ludvigson, Steindel and Lettau (2002, hereafter LSL), who measure the wealth channel by "switching off" the response of consumption to wealth in a structural VAR. The protocol was publicly registered before any data were downloaded, and the five later amendments were dated ahead of the results that could have motivated them.

There are four results. First, the LSL identification is locally but not globally identified: it admits two solutions with the same likelihood, and the second implies explosive dynamics with no economic interpretation. Second, under the solution with weak contemporaneous feedback, the LSL result replicates on every criterion with revised data. Third, extended to 2026, the contribution of the wealth channel to the consumption response remains indistinguishable from zero, including the period in which equities carry their largest weight in household wealth. Fourth, the composition test, which had sufficient precision under the criterion fixed in advance, turns out to be not evaluable: neither equity wealth nor housing wealth responds to the monetary shock in a way distinguishable from zero, so the consumption moved by each dollar of revaluation cannot be measured.

That last result matches Test 1a (Mateos 2026), which used a different method, a different identification and half the sample. In both cases the limit lies in the first link: with aggregate quarterly data, it is not possible to measure precisely how much monetary policy revalues each type of wealth.

detail.abstract: This paper develops the Triple-H Continuum, a relational theory holding that poverty deepens and persists when health deprivation (H1), housing insecurity (H2), and the denial of usable human rights (H3) generate and reinforce one another across time, place, institutions, and unequal relations of power. Existing multidimensional approaches establish that deprivations co-occur; they rarely theorise how deprivation travels from one domain to another, what sustains that movement, and what interrupts it. The paper makes five contributions. First, it specifies each domain conceptually and offers an operational definition of usable rights as a weakest-link function of access, claimability, protection, and remedy. Second, it formalises the continuum as a dynamic system in which a transmission matrix carries deprivation across domains, so that persistent poverty corresponds to a spectral condition on that matrix and total harm decomposes into a sum over transmission pathways. Third, it models six generative mechanisms (dependency, displacement, fragmentation, silencing, cumulative harm, and intergenerational transmission) and the interruptive capacity of voice, exit, and remedy as parameters acting on that system. Fourth, it derives eight falsifiable propositions and an identification strategy that combines panel estimation, Markov transition analysis, and participatory life-history methods. Fifth, it grounds the theory empirically, showing how photovoice can observe cross-domain pathways and mapping the model onto published evidence on migrant workers in Malaysia, where a closed loop between health screening, irregular status and exclusion from care is already documented. The theory positions poverty not as a static stock of deficits but as a process of relational production, and it reframes intervention as coordinated interruption and repair.

detail.abstract: Relative to the persistent delinquency typically observed in consumer credit, mortgage forbearance during the COVID-19 pandemic was surprisingly short-lived. detail.abstract:
This paper evaluates the impact of the pay transparency law on labor outcomes. We
use an equilibrium model with subjective beliefs to illustrate how wage beliefs affect job
search behavior and outcomes. Under the assumptions that women have lower wage
beliefs than comparable men and that more wage information in job postings reduces
the gender gap in wage beliefs, the model predicts that the pay transparency law will
decrease the gender wage gap. Using CPS data and a difference-in-differences design,
we find that the law modestly reduced overall wages—driven primarily by a decline in
male wages among employer stayers. Consistent with the model, the gender wage gap
narrowed sharply among employer changers, falling from 17.5% to 3.5%. This decline
was primarily driven by rising female wages; male wages also fell modestly, though the
decline was not statistically significant. Despite a noticeable effect on the gender wage
gap for job changers, pay transparency did not affect the gender gap in job mobility,
employment, or labor force participation.

detail.abstract: Despite high residential heating and cooling emissions, many households struggle to maintain thermal comfort. Currently, minimum standards for thermal comfort rely heavily on expert consensus and lack deliberative citizen input that weighs comfort against environmental and economic costs. Therefore, we applied Doyal and Gough’s (1991) dual strategy to establish a social floor for the residential thermal environment. We operationalised this strategy by integrating expert knowledge and documented lived experiences within citizen-led focus group discussions (FGDs). Through collective reasoning, participants proposed maximum and minimum thresholds for two need satisfiers: thermal sensation vote (TSV) and indoor temperature. Exceeding maximum or falling below minimum thresholds indicates conditions that hinder meeting human needs.Substantial differences in thermal preferences and normative reasoning prevented full consensus within the FGDs. To establish the social floor, we aggregated participants' proposed thresholds both within and across the independent groups. The minimum TSV thresholds reflect participants' cultural association of warmth with well-being. In contrast, participants compromised thermal comfort more when setting maximum TSV thresholds to limit economic and environmental costs. Minimum TSV thresholds are close to neutral, while the maximum thresholds range from warm to no standard. The daytime minimum and maximum temperatures are 17.8 °C and 28.9 °C, and the nighttime minimum and maximum are 9.6 °C and 26.1 °C. This social floor is less comfortable than most experts' standards, partly because participants expected behavioural adaptations and climate-resilient public spaces to mitigate residential thermal conditions. Consequently, facilitating both adaptation strategies should be part of residential thermal comfort policies.

detail.abstract: The Theory of Human Centrality (TCH), originally formulated in Portuguese as the Teoria da Centralidade Humana, is proposed as a general theory of law organized around a distinction between normative autonomy and epistemic self-sufficiency. Law retains authority to define validity, rights, duties, competences, responsibilities and legal consequences, yet that authority does not entail exclusive capacity to explain the human phenomena on which legal decisions depend. TCH places the person at the integrating center of fact, value, norm, interpretation, decision and consequence and from that premise develops a system composed of epistemic insufficiency, human antecedence of the fact, necessary scientific integration, correspondence between power and cognition, human consequences, continuity of state responsibility and the TCH Test of Epistemic Necessity. The test uses relevance, reliability, materiality, necessity and proportionality to determine when external scientific knowledge ceases to be optional enrichment and becomes part of a legally responsible duty of cognition. The theory does not transfer normative authority to experts, does not equate explanation with exculpation and does not authorize unlimited state inquiry. It instead seeks a controlled form of epistemic openness capable of reducing decisions founded on hidden intuition, misunderstood science, or insufficient factual premises. This foundational preprint reconstructs the intellectual problem addressed by TCH, presents its architecture and principal mechanisms, distinguishes it from generic interdisciplinarity and neighboring approaches, specifies limits and rival explanations and proposes pathways for comparative and empirical testing across adjudication, legislation, public policy and algorithmic decision-making.

Executive Summary: Community water fluoridation has been a cornerstone of U.S. public health for over 75 years and is recognized by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as one of the ten greatest public health achievements of the 20th century (Koppaka, 2011). Illinois, which has mandated fluoridation since 1967, ranks fourth nationally with over 98% of residents receiving fluoridated water (CDC, 2022). However, scrutiny has intensified. A 2024 federal court labeled current fluoride exposure an “unreasonable risk” (Food & Water Watch, Inc. v. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2024). In 2025, 21 states introduced anti-fluoridation bills, and Illinois HB 4321 would allow local opt-outs (Illinois General Assembly, 2025). This brief examines the potential consequences of removing community water fluoridation for policymakers, public health agencies, health care systems, and residents, with particular focus on Illinois populations at elevated risk for dental caries (i.e., cavities).

What does the evidence show?

Extensive evidence shows that community water fluoridation reduces dental caries in children and adults, even with widespread fluoride toothpaste use, and is highly cost-effective—each dollar invested yields $32 in avoided dental costs, with projected national savings of $6.7 billion (O'Connell et al., 2016). Oral disease also imposes substantial societal costs, including roughly 51 million lost school hours and 92 million lost work hours annually; more than 100 health organizations endorse fluoridation as an effective population-level intervention (Koppaka, 2011).

At the same time, a 2024 National Toxicology Program (NTP) report concluded that higher fluoride exposures—typically above 1.5 mg/L—are associated with lower IQ in children, though evidence at standard U.S. fluoridation levels (0.7 mg/L) remains mixed. The National Academies found that neurodevelopmental effects at community water levels are not convincingly demonstrated, underscoring uncertainty around dose and cumulative exposure. These uncertainties, combined with the 2024 federal court ruling, have heightened public concern and spurred legislative action nationwide.

Policy Options for Illinois

If Illinois reconsiders its fluoridation mandate, policymakers should proactively address impacts on oral health systems and population outcomes.

· Strengthen the dental safety net. Expand capacity at safety-net providers—including academic health centers and federally qualified health centers—and increase Medicaid reimbursement to boost dentist participation, especially in rural counties with the greatest access gaps. This would better serve Medicaid-enrolled children and adults and rural residents facing barriers to routine and specialty care.

· Invest in alternative prevention strategies. If fluoridation is reduced or eliminated, Illinois could partially offset impacts by expanding school-based dental sealants, increasing fluoride varnish access through pediatric primary care, and strengthening nutrition programs such as WIC and SNAP. These interventions are resource intensive and unlikely to match fluoridation’s reach or cost-effectiveness.

· Plan for increased surgical demand. Anticipating more children needing treatment under general anesthesia, the state should expand operating room capacity, enhance workforce training, and coordinate medical and dental care. Without preparation, children may face prolonged pain, infection, repeated emergency visits, and multiple surgeries, with high rates of recurrent decay within 12–24 months.

· Monitor outcomes and advance equity. Strengthen oral health surveillance to track disease burden and service use, particularly among Medicaid-enrolled children, rural populations, and communities lacking fluoridated water. Linking data to policy decisions allows timely course correction and helps prevent exacerbation of oral health inequities.

detail.abstract: The concept of hitting bottom occupies a contested position in psychiatric classification and narratives of personal transformation. This paper examines how this concept exposes the classic divide articulated by Karl Jaspers between causal, biological explanation and the phenomenological understanding of subjective meaning. By placing digital peer accounts from r/stopdrinking in dialogue with historical memoirs and clinical literature, alongside Tolstoy as an archetype of non-chemical meaning collapse, we trace how existential crisis operates as a threshold of personal transformation rather than a mere metric of diagnostic severity. Drawing on Dąbrowski, Längle, and Lacan, we map the narrative boundaries of these models to compare the lived stories of recovery with the diagnostic categories of clinical psychiatry. Existential hitting bottom is characterized by an arc of meaning collapse leading to subjective surrender, distinguished from bodily stabilization and incremental adaptation. This comparison outlines a boundary typology that clarifies how psychiatric practice can integrate existential transformation alongside harm reduction, setting out the structural conditions under which different interpretive models resonate.

detail.abstract: I study the macroeconomic and financial spillovers of U.S. monetary policy to Latin America using monthly data for Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru (1994-2019). Identification relies on the set of state-of-the-art high-frequency U.S. monetary policy shocks identified by Bauer and Swanson (2023b). I use local projections in panel and country-specific settings to trace dynamic responses over short and long horizons. I find that a Fed tightening depresses commodity prices and global risk appetite, widens sovereign spreads, depreciates Latin American currencies, and triggers equity sell-offs. detail.abstract: We study the problem of allocating indivisible chores with additive costs, seeking allocations that are weighted envy-free up to one chore (WEF1) and fractionally Pareto optimal (fPO). Mahara (SODA 2026) recently proved that such allocations always exist, but finding one in polynomial time for general instances remains open. For every fixed constant s, we give a polynomial-time algorithm when there are n agents and m ≤ n + s chores. This guarantee allows for arbitrarily many agents and arbitrarily many distinct cost functions. Our approach proceeds through the prescribed quota problem. For a quota vector q, let S(q) denote the number of chores assigned beyond the first chore in each nonempty bundle. We decide whether there is a WEF1 and fPO allocation respecting q, and compute one if it exists, in time m^S(q) · poly(n, m). The algorithm relies on two structural observations: with positive costs and fixed bundle sizes, fPO is equivalent to minimizing the product of assigned costs; and agents who receive at most one chore impose no nontrivial WEF1 constraints. We complement the algorithm with a hardness result showing that the prescribed quota problem becomes strongly NP-hard when S(q) is unbounded, even with two agent types and quotas restricted to {3, 5}.

detail.abstract:
In the sub-sovereign public sector, represented by local governments and police administration, internal reporting systems have fallen into severe dysfunction. Its core lies in structural contradictions at the initial intake stage: through the reversed application of norms and the intentional evasion of fact-finding, misconduct and whistleblowing are not generated as records in the first place. This paper argues that this "non-creation of records" is not an accumulation of frontline negligence or moral hazard, but has become entrenched as a lawful means of organizational defence. Discarding ethical and behavioural approaches, it adopts a Pure Legal System Approach built on three comparative axes: the locus of the burden of proof, external coercive power, and the duty to intervene.

Contrasting Japanese law with the reversal of the burden of proof in the EU Whistleblowing Directive (2019/1937), the consent decrees of the US Department of Justice, and Japan's own legislation for private markets, namely Article 226 of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act and labour administration, the paper shows that these architectures are excluded from the public sector. Under the Whistleblower Protection Act, the Consumer Affairs Agency is limited to instructing whistleblowers, under Article 14, towards investigative agencies, an instruction with no force to bind them. Article 58 of the Local Public Service Act strips external agencies of coercive intervention, and the reversed application of Articles 63 and 65 of the Criminal Investigation Norms legalizes the non-creation of records at initial intake.

The accountability gap is therefore the result of a meticulously designed double standard: a designed vacuum of intervention. Because records are never generated, audits register no issues, and invisible residual losses accumulate that end-investors in JPY-denominated investment-grade bonds, such as local government bonds, and the ESG market cannot price.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the world has entered a regime of structurally higher inflation driven by three mutually reinforcing forces: (i) a reserve-currency hegemon whose public debt now exceeds $40 trillion and is cheapest to service by eroding its real value; (ii) the largest private capital-formation wave since the railways, the AI build-out, which spends roughly $700 billion a year in 2026 on physically scarce inputs; and (iii) a US-China rivalry that turns that spending into a matter of state will rather than market return. The well-known part of the story is that fiat money loses purchasing power over time. The new contribution is the AI Capital Deepening Shock: front-loaded AI investment creates demand today and supply only later, and it collides with inelastic inputs (electricity, memory chips, copper, electricians). Because geopolitics makes this spending price-insensitive, it raises the inflation floor rather than producing a one-off spike. We formalize the argument in a simple debt-dynamics framework, present evidence from official and market sources, and draw one central implication: in this regime, idle cash is the asset most certain to lose, while productive real assets in the hegemon and its allies are the default store of value. We close with the counterarguments that could falsify the thesis.

detail.abstract: External adjustment frameworks assume the state can observe and condition the interface through which residents obtain international settlement. Dollar stablecoins break that assumption at the margin, and they do so before conventional dollarization statistics move, since those statistics measure balance sheets while the change occurs in settlement channels. We name this capacity settlement sovereignty, the ability to observe, exclude, condition, and direct dollar settlement. We measure its erosion in Bolivia around a dated June 2024 authorization that gives the migrating margin a measurable form, drawing on the central bank's published surveillance of platform USDT purchases on Binance, a financial market infrastructure oversight record, alongside the supervisor's bank level reporting on the currency of deposits. By December 2024 monthly platform purchases had quadrupled to USD 31.7 million, an annual pace near USD 380 million set against ex gold reserves that had fallen to USD 87 million. The foreign currency share of the regulated payment rails breaks in April 2023, fourteen months before the parallel premium and well before inflation. Deposit dollarization falls rather than rises. A bank level difference in differences identifies the move as a settlement flight rather than a portfolio shift, concentrated in the transactional deposits that clear payments rather than the term deposits held to store value. The rail share therefore serves as an early, monthly observable marker of settlement migration for payment system oversight. Argentina, Nigeria, and Egypt then serve as boundary cases, probing the persistence, excludability, and financing margins of the Bolivian case. The paper draws out the consequences for reserve adequacy, capital flow management at the interface, and IMF program design.

detail.abstract: This paper asks how the institutional implications of climate change change once the canonical symmetric global-public-good model is embedded in a heterogeneous, dynamic, multi-sector, multi-gas world economy with uncertainty, political economy, incomplete enforcement, trade leakage, endogenous innovation, climate finance, adaptation, non-state actors, burden sharing, common shocks, measurement uncertainty, and scale-dependent governance costs. The empirical foundation is a reproducible SQLite corpus harmonizing eighteen sources spanning EDGAR 2026 annual and monthly greenhouse-gas emissions, World Development Indicators, Penn World Table 11.0, the Global Macro Database, IMF Air Emissions Accounts, Global Forest Watch tree-cover loss, and World Bank commodity prices. The reduced-form evidence continues to support a planetary scale mismatch: fossil CO₂ rises from 15.2 Gt in 1970 to 38.6 Gt in 2025, the geographic distribution of emissions shifts sharply away from Annex I, the largest emitters remain highly concentrated, and monthly changes contain a strong common international component. The structural extension, the Dynamic Multilevel Planetary Governance model, initializes the 40 largest 2025 emitters plus a residual world agent from the corpus and runs annual counterfactuals through 2100. Sectoral autonomous decarbonization is anchored to 2000–2025 EDGAR emissions-intensity trends; CH₄, N₂O, and F-gases are modeled separately; growth and population converge rather than extrapolating recent rates indefinitely; tipping risk, adaptation, clean-technology spillovers, endogenous climate-club participation, border adjustments, budget-balanced transfers, lobbying, electoral cycles, non-state implementation, and institutional costs are explicit. The resulting paths show that stronger supranational coordination can reduce model-implied emissions and climate damages while also changing leakage, transfers, innovation, adaptation, and institutional resource costs. Because several political and institutional parameters are proxy-calibrated or scenario-based, these counterfactuals are not causal historical estimates and are not used to rank constitutional forms. The combined evidence supports a planetary-scale internalization problem; the institutional form used to solve it remains a conditional comparative question.

detail.abstract:
This working paper explores the impact of automation and AI on decision making within the public sector. The approach taken is “green light” emphasising the need for governments to govern and the advantages that technology can bring to executive functions. In taking this approach, the paper attempts to move beyond a focus on the inability of technologies (particularly related to machine learning) to operate within the contexts of administrative law. Instead, it argues for a focus upon the purpose of administrative law and how it can be adapted to address the challenge of new technologies.

Nevertheless, such a green light approach has limits. This paper argues that the very nature of public activities means that the claimed efficiencies of technological advancement in general (and machine learning in particular) cannot be used to trump the essential legitimacy required of these functions. If such technologies cannot be delivered in a way that satisfies the requirements of public legitimacy (however that is defined) then they cannot be utilised in a public context. If this incompatibility cannot be resolved, then no amount of efficiency gains can override the public imperative. However, by taking a functional (green light) approach to law, administration and automation, this paper suggests that, while some areas of government policy must remain outside the automated realm, in others good administrative practice can operate alongside an increasingly automated state.

detail.abstract: The surge of concerns about foreign interference has prompted a wave of regulatory responses across democracies. In the EU, the 2023 Defence of Democracy package and the proposed Directive on transparency of interest representation on behalf of third countries are the flagship initiatives of this wave. In this paper, I examine the Directive through a comparative lens, contrasting it with the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and the repressive foreign agent laws adopted by authoritarian regimes. Drawing on the evolving roles of NGOs as transnational legal actors, the analysis highlights how the Directive abandons the traditional distinction between lobbying and advocacy, recognizing the inherently political nature of NGO activity while deliberately avoiding the stigmatizing language of foreign-agent laws. I argue that this approach, which seeks to legitimize the Directive through transparency, is welcome but conflates foreign influence with foreign interference. The paper further argues that by relying on transparency, the Directive attempts to produce a "democratic sufficit": rather than addressing the structural accountability gaps that enable foreign interference, the Commission treats NGO registration as a substitute for the deeper institutional reforms and genuine citizen mobilization that democratic legitimacy requires. Transparency, examined through the lens of EU constitutional law and CJEU case law, cannot bear the weight the Directive places on it.

detail.abstract: We show that inflation expectations of households causally depend on remembered rather than actually experienced inflation rates. Specifically, we asked German households for their remembered average and peak inflation rates and investigate how inflation experiences are formed and what they depend on. We establish five facts: (i) What matters for expectations is what households believe they have lived through, which cannot be proxied well by actual circumstances. (ii) On average, households overestimate current and lifetime inflation, although they are mostly confident in their estimates. (iii) Negative emotions associated with inflation raise the bias in perception and memory. (iv) High inflation rates are perceived and remembered more correctly. (v) Higher remembered inflation rates cause higher inflation expectations. We present a theoretical model that accounts for the empirical evidence.

detail.abstract:
Each technological revolution triggers rivalry to command the material base on which the new economy runs. The first Industrial Revolution, which introduced a scalable substitute for manual labour, drove the original “scramble for Africa” as the industrializing powers sought to secure industrial inputs, including inter alia rubber, palm oil and gold (in the case of the latter, to expand the monetary base under the gold standard to ward of deflation as production soared); and to establish captive markets for their rapidly scaling manufacturing output. This first “scramble” was formalized at the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885, which partitioned Africa. No African state was represented in Berlin. 

The current technological revolution, which is introducing a scalable substitute for human mental labour in the form of generative/agentic artificial intelligence (AI as “machine knowledge capital”), has triggered a new scramble, this time for data and the critical minerals that are indispensable to the physical infrastructure of the new age – computer chips, memory, batteries, magnets, electric power, telecommunications (including subsea cables, low-earth orbit satellites, and the next-gen local edge compute networks to power autonomous mobile devices), and data centres. Africa, holding roughly 30% of the world’s reserves of the critical minerals required to build out this infrastructure, is again at the centre of attention. 

The study argues that the decisive feature distinguishing the present “scramble for Africa” from the first is that this time Africa has agency, partnership options, and a keen awareness of the economic returns implicit in the emerging commodity supercycle driven by the capital-expenditure-intensive era of machine knowledge capital and the green transition.  The United States faces a policy lemma: rising tariffs and uncertainty about access to the U.S. market and sharply reduced development engagement have effectively distanced it from African economies even as these seek to capture value as a participant in the new economy.  To be a legitimate contender in the new “scramble,” the new “pivot” the United States must consider is towards partnership, soft power, and a resurrection of a win-win long-term framing of its relationship with Africa. A good place to start is critical minerals.

detail.abstract: We develop an ex post approach to sufficientarianism under risk that is based on the notion of expected representative utility. Sufficientarianism is a theory of distributive justice that, in the form considered here, grants absolute priority to individuals below a sufficiency threshold. Expected representative-utility criteria satisfy weak Pareto for equal risk in the case of prioritarianism, but this axiom conflicts with the absolute priority principle. However, by restricting weak Pareto for equal risk to apply separately within the subdomains above and below the threshold, and by weakening continuity accordingly, we obtain a characterization of the expected representative-utility sufficientarian orderings. Our main theorem establishes that these orderings are characterized by ex post absolute priority, restricted versions of weak Pareto for no risk and of weak Pareto for equal risk, statewise dominance, and restricted continuity axioms. For populations of at least three individuals, we further characterize a subclass based on quasiarithmetic means by imposing strong Pareto for no risk and adding anonymity and outcome independence of the unconcerned to the list of axioms. We also establish that, within this subclass, only the arithmetic expected representative-utility sufficientarian ordering satisfies prospect independence of the unconcerned, a stronger axiom of independence.

detail.abstract: Rapid catch-up growth insures risk taking. When modern activity expands quickly, a person whose venture fails returns to productive work sooner, so failure is cheap and many people are willing to migrate, switch occupations, or start firms. I build a model in which realized catchup growth is the product of the distance to the technology frontier and the share of agents who experiment, and in which expansion raises the re-entry hazard after failure. Experimentation and expansion reinforce each other, but the complementarity is proportional to the remaining distance, so successful catch-up erodes the insurance that sustained it. The elasticity of participation with respect to expansion organizes the dynamics, and the two points at which it equals one determine the geometry. If the catch-up growth needed to keep pace with the frontier lies above the upper point, convergence is smooth. If it lies below the lower point, catch-up ends in a sharp slowdown, possibly after the economy has overshot its long-run relative income. If it lies between them, the steady state can be unstable when participation adjusts quickly relative to the gap, and the economy alternates between catch-up and relative decline. Formal insurance substitutes for growth insurance: it lowers the long-run gap, postpones the slowdown, and, when strong enough, removes the discontinuity. Its value is larger the slower catch-up expansion is.

detail.abstract: Crude-oil commercial decisions are often initiated months before physical delivery, while related commitments may be revised on any trading day as market conditions evolve. This creates a forecasting setting in which the price outlook extends several months ahead while the information supporting that outlook is updated daily. We address this setting by producing daily forecasts of the three-month-ahead WTI cash price (hereafter, spot price). The highly liquid WTI futures market provides a strong benchmark for this target, while the futures term structure offers additional cross-maturity information and evolves daily before the corresponding spot-price outcome becomes available. This delayed-feedback structure motivates a framework that starts from a maturity-aligned futures benchmark and learns from historical daily curve dynamics. detail.abstract: This study investigates which structural vulnerability in contemporary accounting most resists efforts to prevent illicit funds from acquiring legitimacy within the economic system. It conceptualises accounting-mediated legitimation (ACCLEG) as the degree to which illicit or economically contested value acquires a formally plausible accounting, documentary, corporate, or financial representation. An exploratory mixed-methods design combines standardised responses from eight large language models, lexical textometry using IRaMuTeQ, documentary analysis of 30 publicly documented financial-crime cases, and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA). Five structural conditions are examined: procedural shielding, beneficial-ownership opacity, data fragmentation, valuation subjectivity, and regulatory rigidity. The documentary evidence shows that procedural shielding and data fragmentation are pervasive, while valuation subjectivity is less frequent but substantially more discriminating. Under the principal fsQCA specification, the intermediate solution is PROC * VAL → ACCLEG, whereas the parsimonious solution reduces to VAL → ACCLEG, with consistency of 0.976 and coverage of 0.617. The results indicate that valuation subjectivity is the core configurational condition associated with high accounting-mediated legitimation, while procedural shielding operates primarily as a contextual condition. The findings extend critical accounting and AML research by showing that the central vulnerability is not always missing information or concealed ownership, but the capacity of formally acceptable representations to confer plausibility on economic value whose substantive basis remains difficult to verify independently. The study interprets this limitation through a restricted Gödelian analogy, conceptualising accounting incompleteness as epistemic and institutional rather than mathematical.

detail.abstract:
For much of the twentieth century, judges administered procedure holistically, balancing speed, administrability, and fairness. But the Roberts Court has increasingly replaced this equitable approach with rigid procedural rules that deliver mechanical yes-or-no answers. I term this new approach, with its erasure of grey areas susceptible to lower-court discretion, “procedural absolutism.” Synthesizing legal history, doctrine, and theory, this Article shows how procedural absolutism unifies the Court's watershed opinions on distinct procedural structures, including personal jurisdiction, remedies, arbitration, choice of law, and notice and hearing.

The Court’s approach to procedure is distinct from its substantive jurisprudence. Despite its claimed adherence to originalism, much of the Roberts Court’s new procedural rules are driven by contemporary policy considerations, with little textual or historical basis. Nor does the jurisprudence of procedural absolutism neatly map onto the Court’s conservative ideology, as a number of the resulting rules expressly disfavor corporations and provide meaningful (if imperfect) opportunities for challenging businesses and the executive branch. Procedural absolutism is best understood, instead, as an extension of the Roberts Court’s confidence that legal questions have objectively correct answers divorced from context, and that the Supreme Court—not lower courts—should be the sole arbiter of these questions.

Ironically, this move toward inflexible procedural rules that yield predictable answers may empower the very parties whom the Court’s conservative substantive jurisprudence has marginalized. Consumers, employees, immigrants, and progressive lawmakers have begun identifying and exploiting workarounds created by the inflexibility of procedural absolutism—a strategy I identify as “procedural opportunism.” This Article demonstrates the potential of procedural opportunism through a number of movements leveraging rigid rigid procedure, including when consumers and employees file mass-arbitration claims to invert the Court’s business-favoring arbitration jurisprudence, when detained immigrants leverage uniform new notice requirements by bringing habeas class actions that quickly halt government removals, and when state legislatures statutorily expand personal jurisdiction to counter the Court’s narrowing of the holistic minimum-contacts test. Thus, even as procedural absolutism limits lower-court discretion to craft equitable processes that account for power asymmetries, it also presents immediate opportunities for combatting corporate abuses and reactionary federal policies.

detail.abstract:
This Essay presents new data on partisan polarization in lower-court implementation of the Roberts Court's campaign-finance jurisprudence. Surveying more than 2,000 federal cases decided between 2005 and 2025 that raised First Amendment speech-clause challenges to a campaign-finance regulation, it builds a dataset to study judicial behavior toward a labile body of deregulatory First Amendment law. It then reflects on what this behavior reveals about the nature and health of constitutional democracy and adjudication as elite party polarization and bimodal sorting pervade Article III courts. 

Among its findings: Democratic appointees ruled in a proregulatory manner in 72.3% of judicial acts and Republican appointees in 41.3%; the partisan gap scales with interpretive latitude, widening from 15.0 percentage points at the district courts to 32.7 at the courts of appeals to 81.5 at the Supreme Court; and intraparty appointee behavior measurably varies by appointing president, with President Trump's nominees an outlier among Republican appointees due to their consistently deregulatory rulings. The more surprising finding is reactive. After Citizens United, Democratic appointees became markedly more protective of regulation, with their full-invalidation rate falling by over a third while Republican appointees' rate held nearly constant. Democratic appointees thus moved against the formal direction that a binding and high-profile deregulatory precedent required. 

The Essay explains this asymmetry through the concept of the "metonymic tripwire," which tracks the creation of anticanonical law in constitutional culture and conflict. It contends that Citizens United acquired a cultural valence and symbolism exceeding its formal legal content by condensing an ideological project into a single interpretive term. When that meaning, built by nonjudicial actors and mediated by broader sociolegal forces, filtered back to the bench, it realigned judicial behavior beyond anything doctrine would predict. The Essay concludes by considering the implications of the documented Article III polarization on the fonts of judicial authority: specifically, law's perceptible separation from politics, the reciprocal exchange between constitutional law and constitutional culture, and the capacity of the First Amendment to serve as a shared constitutional inheritance.

detail.abstract: I propose establishing a single, external and independent authority to verify the integrity of Venezuelan debt claims before their final admission to a restructuring. Its role would be to determine which obligations are recognized, who receives their economic benefits, and what documentation establishes how each position was acquired and financed. The rationale for this authority lies in bringing together frameworks that currently operate separately. The Palermo and Mérida Conventions provide the criminal law framework and mechanisms for judicial cooperation, while the FATF Recommendations establish preventive standards and call for coordination among domestic authorities. The Basel Committee's principles and guidelines apply a risk-based approach to the institutions that would settle the exchange. The EU's 2024 legislative package and the Swiss reform in force since 1 October 2026 regulate access to beneficial ownership information in jurisdictions that may form part of a position's ownership and custody chain. The Egmont Group's Principles, whose third revision was approved by Heads of Financial Intelligence Units in July 2025, provide a channel through which financial intelligence may reach a competent authority for a stated purpose. None of these instruments establishes the proposed authority. This article explains how enabling legislation, the contractual terms of the exchange and cooperation agreements could translate those frameworks into specific powers. I retain, as a political prerequisite, a legitimate government formed through elections, and envisage the IMF's role in rebuilding statistical capacity and developing the macroeconomic program within which the exchange would take place.

detail.abstract: Financial accountability is essential in public education, where personnel manage government funds to sustain school operations and ensure transparency in resource utilization. This study examined the financial management competencies of non-teaching personnel and their compliance with liquidation requirements in a school district in Sarangani, Philippines. Competencies were assessed across six dimensions: budgeting and financial planning, bookkeeping and financial recording, cash management and disbursement, procurement and documentation, internal control and accountability, and financial reporting and monitoring. Compliance was measured in terms of timeliness of liquidation, completeness of supporting documents, accuracy of financial reports, adherence to accounting and auditing procedures, and conformity with prescribed regulations. Employing a quantitative descriptive-correlational design, the study involved a total population of 50 non-teaching personnel in the subject school district. Data gathered through researcher-structured questionnaire were analyzed using frequency and percentage distributions, weighted mean, and Spearman's rank-order correlation. Results revealed that respondents rated their financial management competencies highly, while compliance with liquidation requirements was largely compliant, though recurring challenges persisted in documentation and timeliness. Significant positive relationships were found between all competency dimensions and liquidation compliance, with financial reporting and monitoring showing the strongest association. Based on these findings, a financial management strategies were developed to strengthen training, internal controls, and monitoring practices. The study underscored the importance of enhancing personnel competencies and compliance mechanisms to improve financial accountability and transparency in Philippine public schools. The results also provide empirical support for Stewardship Theory, extending its application to non-teaching personnel directly responsible for financial and liquidation functions.

detail.abstract: Stablecoins are commonly classified according to their issuers’ stated design, such as fiatbacked, crypto-backed, or algorithmic. This note asks whether they also sort into discrete behavioral types. We examine 111 stablecoins that survived and were adequately observed through the first 180 days after first sustaining $1 million in the issuance record. Six behavioral measures are calculated using observations from days 0 to 179 only, so subsequent outcomes do not enter the measurement. Three rotated principal components explain 95% of the variance and capture local peg stability, supply trajectory, and supply volatility. We test for discrete groups using an explicitly stated decision rule calibrated on simulated samples of the same size, including 2,000 draws from a Gaussian-copula continuum preserving the empirical marginals and planted three-group mixtures of known separation. The observed data do not satisfy the rule: cluster separation remains within the continuum reference range at every partition size, the overlap-penalized mixture criterion selects one component, and no partition’s bootstrap reproducibility exceeds its continuum reference. The rule’s false-positive rate is 0.1%; it detects planted groups separated by four standard deviations of the leading component in 99% of simulations and by three in 15%. Declared backing category explains 4% of score variance in the fiat-backed versus cryptobacked comparison (permutation p = 0.006). Fiat-backed coins are more stable around local par, with less drawdown and stronger supply growth. Within this population, coins are better described by their position on continuous coordinates than by membership in behavioral types; groups separated by three standard deviations or less would not usually be detected.

detail.abstract:
Multi-country issuance (MCI) allows the same stablecoin to be issued by legally separate entities in different jurisdictions while circulating as a single, technologically fungible token. This structure creates a specific risk for Europe: in a run, holders can direct redemptions towards the jurisdiction offering the fastest, cheapest or legally safest exit. Because MiCAR provides stronger and less flexible redemption rights than the emerging US regime, dollar-stablecoin runs originating elsewhere may concentrate on the EU issuer. 

Current European proposals do not remove this incentive. Restrictions based on holder location or intermediary status, dedicated liquidity buffers, reserve mobility and formal equivalence may raise access costs or strengthen redemption capacity, but they leave the EU channel relatively more attractive and may prove difficult to enforce under stress. 

If Europe continues to permit MCI, MiCAR should instead seek functional redemption equivalence with the US regime. We propose automatic stabilisers embedded in the redemption infrastructure: charges once outflows cross an initial threshold, followed by temporary gates at more extreme levels. These measures would reduce self-fulfilling redemptions and prevent the EU issuer from becoming the default outlet for dollar-run pressure. An exceptional ECB power to suspend redemptions should remain available where contingent measures cannot contain systemic outflows. This framework would protect European financial stability, strategic autonomy and monetary sovereignty.

detail.abstract: Stablecoin issuers hold the same short-term safe assets that banks must hold to meet liquidity rules; we ask when issuance starts to crowd out bank collateral. Theoretically, we model banks that comply with the liquidity coverage ratio every day at a cost— covering shortfalls with term funding or the discount window up to their pledgeable collateral and deleveraging beyond it. The price of collateral then rises smoothly with issuance, and the regulatory threshold is the midpoint of a crowding-out zone rather than its start. Two channels operate: issuers’ bill purchases remove collateral from the system, and issuer deposits raise the precautionary demand of the banks that receive them; bills crowd out more than deposits. Because coin demand rises as bill yields fall, there can be a fold, a largest demand beyond which issuance growing from today’s stock does not settle; where it lies depends on how issuers and coin holders respond. In the US calibration the premium on safe assets is 3 basis points at today’s stock of $311 billion, 25 at a total stock of $661 billion and 100 at $1,036 billion, against a regulatory threshold of $961 billion. With the observed reserve mix the fold is at a demand of $1,949 billion; it moves to $2.0–3.1 trillion when issuers shift toward deposits, which pay more than bills once collateral is scarce, and it disappears when coin holders’ alternative is a bank deposit. Discount-window readiness and a Federal Reserve deposit share for issuers that is lent back to banks raise welfare most and are tied at $1 trillion of demand; reserves held as bank deposits come next; an issuance cap lowers welfare wherever it binds; and run-off rates on issuer deposits and concentration limits mainly address the run externality. Empirically, every bank that held Circle’s cash before March 2023 was outside the liquidity coverage ratio; Silvergate held liquidity against its issuer deposits as a narrow bank would, and the model’s capital condition singles it out among partner banks; the ratios of the twenty-one bank holding companies under the rule have not fallen below 1.04 since 2018, as a probabilistic compliance cost implies; and bill-buying issuer dollars lower three-month bill yields by 10.8–19.1 basis points per $3.5 billion for a few weeks, while the same issuers’ repo and deposit dollars do not.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the efficiency cost of pay-as-you-go pension systems. The return on pension contributions-typically average income growth-is lower than the market return on capital. Because the gap between these returns compounds over the life cycle, early-career contributions have a higher implicit tax rate. I develop a sufficient-statistics framework in which the deadweight loss depends on the age profile of implicit tax rates. Deadweight loss is minimized when the implicit tax rate is constant, mirroring the logic of tax smoothing. I then propose an implementation within a notional defined contribution design: contributions are valorized at a higher, market-based rate of return, while a lower fraction of contributions is credited to notional accounts and the remainder treated as a pure tax. Finally, I apply my deadweight loss formula to OECD PAYGO pension systems. Under the assumed parameter values, the deadweight loss averages 19 percent. I find that only 0.2 percentage points is attributable to the uneven timing of implicit taxation.

detail.abstract: Environmental improvements can benefit people outside the country undertaking them, yet domestic policy appraisals can overlook these spillover benefits. detail.abstract: Behavioral responses to environmental stressors can mitigate damages when risks are observable and correctly diagnosed. However, when the underlying stressor is hidden and difficult to diagnose, responses based on observed symptoms may be less effective and may even be misdirected. We examine this possibility in U.S. agriculture by studying whether exposure to ground-level ozone, a colorless and odorless pollutant that impairs photosynthesis and produces symptoms resembling nutrient deficiency or pest and disease stress, leads to factor misallocation. To do so, we integrate remote-sensing, statistical, and survey data in a county fixed effects framework that instruments local ozone exposure with upwind ozone levels. We first confirm ozone's well-established direct yield damage and then document ozone-induced factor misallocation, reflected in higher fertilizer and pesticide use, while inputs unrelated to nutrient or pest stress, such as machinery, remain unaffected. These misallocations are attenuated in counties with greater information access, higher education levels, or more experienced producers. The misallocation loss from a one ppb increase in ozone amounts to roughly $1.24 billion per year, equivalent to approximately 69% of the direct yield loss. These findings suggest that policies that improve ozone awareness and diagnostic capacity can complement pollution-control efforts by reducing avoidable losses from misdirected input responses.

detail.abstract: Public flagship universities increasingly use nonresident tuition revenues to offset declining state funding. Nationally, we find that public flagships facing lower state support enroll relatively more high-income nonresidents. We then link two decades of University of Alabama (UA) commencement records to admissions office recruiting visits and individual employment histories. These data allow us to document how universities pursue this revenue margin and to measure downstream effects on graduates and state budgets. We show UA boosts high-income out-of-state demand through targeted recruitment visits: in a differences-in-differences design, new visits generate 8–10 percent more future UA graduates. We then trace how nonresident enrollment redirects graduates across state labor markets. Using variation in the state-of-origin composition of UA cohorts and a shift-share instrument constructed from origin states' non-UA out-of-state enrollment rates, we estimate that every 100 out-of-state students cause 9–15 additional in-state students to leave the state after college. These patterns are consistent with peer effects operating through expanded consideration sets and referral networks. The resulting fiscal losses to Alabama exceed the university's nonresident tuition margins. Finally, the out-of-state expansion appears to support in-state degree production. A budget accounting exercise shows that UA's out-of-state enrollment margins are sufficient to cross-subsidize more than half of the in-state cohort, who receive an average annual subsidy of $13,000 per student.

detail.abstract: Are housing policies progressive? We study this question in an equilibrium model where low-income households sort into old units at the bottom of the housing ladder. We show that price changes along the ladder are a sufficient statistic for welfare changes across the income distribution. Policy propagates to prices through the affordability effect, which moves demand along the ladder, and the tear-down effect, which shifts supply at the bottom. The progressivity of specific policies depends on their loadings on each effect. Policy can also cause construction peaks and troughs, inducing vintage effects which further shape progressivity along a transition. We take the model to the data, calibrating to a representative US city. Our findings suggest that construction subsidies are regressive, especially in the short run. Maintenance subsidies emerge as a progressive alternative.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for understanding how economic dependence can shape Canadian sovereignty. Canada's deep economic integration with the United States creates an asymmetric dependence that gives the U.S. bargaining power over Canada. The United States cannot credibly commit to forgo the use of this power because promises between sovereign states cannot be perfectly enforced. However, constitutional integration changes this commitment problem by replacing a relationship between sovereign countries with one in which executive power is constrained by domestic constitutional law. Canada therefore faces three broad options: accepting concessions, undertaking costly trade diversification, or pursuing constitutional integration. Domestic disagreement over the value of sovereignty may lead Canada to underdiversify its trading relationships, while Quebec's distinct national identity means that constitutional proposals recognizing Quebec sovereignty may attract greater support than uniform statehood proposals.

detail.abstract: Africa's shift towards intangible and digital economic activity creates a distinctive taxadministration problem. Intellectual property generates cross-border value through royalties, licensing, trademarks and software, yet its ownership, location, valuation and exploitation are difficult for revenue authorities to identify and verify. At the other end of the market, creators earn income from streaming, licensing, sponsorship and platforms, while much of the creative economy remains outside formal tax and reporting systems. Although multinational profit shifting and creator informality arise from different institutional and behavioural conditions, both expose a common weakness: limited capacity to identify, value, attribute and trace income derived from intangible assets. The article develops the concept of the intangible tax gap and undertakes a comparative doctrinal and policy analysis of Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, covering the taxation of royalties and other IP-derived income, withholding, transfer pricing for intangibles and creator formalisation. It argues that IP infrastructure, including registries, collective management reporting and IP-finance systems, can contribute to tax visibility by linking ownership, exploitation, valuation and income data, while recognising the privacy costs and the risks of inflated valuations, artificial licensing and illicit financial flows. It proposes an Intangible Tax Governance Framework built on risk-based, proportionate enforcement and a creator regularisation mechanism with anti-abuse safeguards. It concludes that effective taxation of Africa's intangible economy requires not only broader tax rules but better institutional infrastructure for making intangible value visible, verifiable and traceable.

detail.abstract: Households respond to recessions by reallocating time and spending across market work, home production, and leisure. In a static framework, we show that countercyclical adjustments partly cushion shocks: skilled households substitute non-market time for market work and reduce expenditures, while unskilled households respond in the opposite direction. These adjustments are stronger across space than over time and more pronounced for home production than leisure, resulting in more volatile marketconsumption and smoother non-market consumption. The mechanisms reflect the interaction of substitution and income effects and the joint role of time and money in consumption. Two limitations temper these mechanisms. Demographic heterogeneity leads some groups to exhibit procyclical adaptations that amplify shocks, and countercyclical adaptations take time to build, constrained by labor market rigidities, household coordination, and liquidity.

detail.abstract: Movements in China’s foreign-exchange reserves may signal both potential demand for safe dollar assets and the broader macro-financial conditions surrounding reserve accumulation. Using monthly data from December 2000 to December 2025, we estimate a three-factor affine term-structure model for US Treasury yields. Reserve growth does not enter contemporaneous yield pricing but can influence yields over time through subsequent movements in the level, slope, and curvature factors. The model decomposes the 10-year yield into an expectations component based on expected future short-term interest rates and a term premium. After controlling for inflation, broad US dollar movements, financial-market uncertainty, and Chinese cyclical conditions, the estimates show that higher reserve growth is followed by a gradual rise in the 10-year Treasury yield. The positive yield response remains after adding international currency-risk controls and using alternative reserve and transaction measures, although its allocation between expectations and term premia varies across measures. Reserve dynamics therefore contain conditional predictive information for Treasury yields, while the decomposition of that information is measurement-dependent. Complementary VAR evidence points to persistent adjustment through the level and slope factors. The findings support interpreting reserve growth as a policy-conditioned macro-financial indicator rather than a direct measure of intervention or official Treasury purchases.

detail.abstract: An agent meets a model as served: through an endpoint with a price card, a shared cache and other tenants, or on whatever hardware a self-hosted model runs. Benchmarks rank the weights. We introduce a Tetris benchmark that measures what agents get from models as served: every move is scored against an oracle, and every agent receives the same pieces. In five pre-specified experiments with nine open-weight models on one serverless provider, plus an open decision model self-hosted on a CPU, we find that price and size do not predict decision quality; that resending history costs almost nothing when cached input is free, would cost eleven to twelve times more if it were not, and makes play worse; that deployments keep between 4 and more than 64 agent contexts warm, in line with their throughput rather than the model's KV-cache size; that an agent's own long requests slow its slowest short decisions more than tenfold, which a simple admission rule cuts by 59% without hurting play; and that the decision model plays mid-pack but takes 27 s per move on a CPU, about 650 times longer than reported on a GPU. detail.abstract: The 1976 Act was the product of extensive negotiations among representatives of copyright insiders. That process predictably disadvantaged parties that were not at the bargaining table. But what about the folks who were represented in the negotiations and involved in crafting the statute’s language? The bargains they made didn’t always work out for them. Sometimes those bargains were predicated on assumptions that turned out to be wrong. Sometimes they were overturned by court rulings misconstruing the language the parties thought they had agreed on. detail.abstract: This paper develops the concept of normative capacity to analyze a growing asymmetry between the capacity of institutions to adapt and the capacity of societies to reconsider the purposes those institutions serve. Improvement always presupposes a criterion, yet highly adaptive institutions can become increasingly effective at pursuing legible criteria even when those criteria no longer track broader human purposes. Drawing on organizational learning, experimentalist governance, political theory, and AI alignment, the paper argues that artificial intelligence can deepen this asymmetry by making adaptation to measurable objectives more continuous and potentially self-reinforcing. Normative capacity is defined as the persistence of institutional mechanisms that keep purposes explicit, contestable, consequential, and answerable to experience. The argument further derives a minimum legitimacy floor preserving practical agency, a requirement of interpretive plurality against normative compression, and a need to couple normative revision to the pace of adaptation. The paper concludes that AI alignment must include continuing institutional capacity to revise objectives, not only technical fidelity to inherited ones.

detail.abstract: Clinical, operational, and financial decisions that are made by hospitals rely on different purposes designed data systems. The care delivery, patient status and clinician action are described with electronic health records, reimbursement and resources consumption described with claims and cost-accounting systems with even more of these views added to the workforce, supply-chain, quality, and patient-experience systems. By having these data segregated, leaders can observe a quality issue or a financial variance but will not be able to reliably relate the same to the episode, workflow, patient risk or operational cause. The paper will create an evidence-based framework of how clinical and financial analytics can be integrated, enhancing a better performance of the hospital and strategic decision-making. It specifies a controlled episode-based data model, a performance measurement system with a balanced performance, and an analytical process between the descriptive reporting and the causal evaluation and constrained optimization. Four illustrations of science depict an interrelationship of some statistics, a broken chart of statistical-process-controversy, an analysis of cost variance by Pareto, and a frontier-service-line quality/finance service-line. All of the numbers used are artificial and not a depiction of a hospital. The structural aspect prioritizes the adjustment of risks, attribution, governing the denominator, timecorrecting data, uncertainty, equity of patients and reconciling the financial records. It additionally makes a distinction between association, prediction and causal evidence so that dashboards do not make assumptions that a correlated measure of operations caused a result. Hospitals must start with a narrowed decision and outcome as compared to an enterprise-wide dashboard. It should be implemented in the following steps that include metric definition, identity, and episode linkage, verification, prospective workflow testing, benefit reconciliation, and continual governance. Capacity planning, service-line strategy, quality improvement, revenue integrity, and resource allocation, can be facilitated with integrated analytics, and their value hinges on trusted data and responsible usage. The framework suggested provides leaders in the hospital sector with a feasible framework to link patient outcomes with the costs and resources they need to achieve results.

detail.abstract: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) has made macroeconomic convergence the precondition for launching the Eco, its proposed common currency, now scheduled for a phased introduction in 2027. This paper tests that strategy against its own record. I assemble a panel of compliance with the ECOWAS convergence criteria for all fifteen member states over 2005–2016, hand-collected from oﬀicial surveillance reports, and merge it with macroeconomic co-variates. Compliance responds to fundamentals in exposure-adjusted count models: disinflation, growth, and stronger external balances all raise the number of criteria met. Yet the cross-country dispersion of compliance widened significantly over the surveillance period, business cycles are unsynchronized (the mean pairwise correlation of real GDP growth is zero, and Nigeria’s cycle is uncorrelated with the rest of the region), and full compliance occurs in only 7 of 180 country-years, every one of them a member of the pre-existing WAEMU currency union in a single year. The criteria therefore select for countries that already share a currency, which reverses the causal logic of the convergence-first strategy. Text-mining the five oﬀicial convergence reports (2010–2016) shows that institutional discourse consolidated sharply as launch deadlines approached even as the underlying data diverged; permutation tests attribute this to genuine narrative re-alignment rather than boilerplate duplication. I draw out the implications for the 2027 phased launch, for criteria design under commodity-price asymmetry, and for a sequencing of integration that places trade, payments, and fiscal insurance before monetary unification.

Higher MSRP levels also persisted after some pandemic-era cost pressures eased. The findings support an interpretation of pricing as the result of multiple cost and market forces rather than simple one-for-one cost pass-through.

detail.abstract: In autumn 2026 the Italian government announced a package of measures for advanced robotics and Physical AI: a dedicated fund of 200-300 million euro in the 2027 budget law, the use of Innovation Agreements (Accordi per l'innovazione) as the delivery vehicle, a publicly controlled "chain leader" to aggregate the supply side, an inter-ministerial committee on labour impacts, and a joint position with France and Germany at European level. This paper argues that the package is necessary but incomplete. It is built on a supply-side logic that finances the production of robotic bodies and the consolidation of a national champion, while leaving unaddressed the problem that has determined the outcome of every Italian technology incentive since 2017: the conversion of purchased capital into productive capacity. Drawing on the final evaluation of the Transizione 4.0 plan, on the evidence on the productivity J-curve, and on the technical literature on humanoid reliability, data scarcity and deployment, the paper identifies the specific features that make Physical AI adoption riskier and more complement-intensive than previous waves of automation. It then proposes a demand-side pillar built around five instruments: a pilot voucher delivered through the existing network of Competence Centres and European Digital Innovation Hubs; a transformation tax credit within the Nuova Transizione 5.0 regime, recognising integration, data and labour costs against a measured baseline; a network of mission testbeds operating under a common evaluation protocol and feeding a national evidence registry; performance-based public first-market contracts; and binding conditions on interoperability, data portability and workforce transition for any platform receiving public money. The paper quantifies the order of magnitude of each instrument, explains how the pillar can be integrated with the announced fund and with the Innovation Agreements without new legislation of general scope, and proposes a set of indicators, including stop rules, to govern the programme. The central claim is that for an immature, learning technology, reducing the risk of adoption is at least as important as reducing the price of the asset, and that the Italian institutional system already possesses most of the components needed to do so. detail.abstract: Firms are increasingly experimenting with LLM-based agents for pricing decisions. We study the reliability of these decisions and develop, to our knowledge, the first analytically tractable framework that links Transformer pretraining to an LLM agent's pricing decisions. We explicitly characterize the weights learned by a pretrained Transformer and use them to derive the agent's demand-estimation rule, its bias and variance, and the resulting pricing regret. The analysis reveals a fundamental limitation: the agent behaves like a "rote learner." Although it can adapt to a new pricing environment using examples supplied in the prompt, the way it interprets those examples remains anchored to the covariate structure encountered during pretraining. As a result, its demand estimates can be systematically biased when the prompt and pretraining covariate distributions are misaligned. Increasing the number of historical examples in the prompt reduces estimation variance and makes the agent's decisions more stable, but does not remove this bias; more context can therefore make the agent more consistent without making it more accurate. This limitation is particularly critical for commercial LLMs because users typically cannot observe the models' pretraining data and hence cannot verify whether the required alignment holds. Numerical experiments with pretrained Transformers, real-world pricing data, and commercial LLMs including GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok provide evidence consistent with these theoretical implications.

detail.abstract: Parametric insurance can pay quickly after a cyclone because payment is linked to a measurable trigger rather than a full loss assessment. Its main challenge is basis risk: the trigger may pay when severe impact is limited or fail to pay when severe impact occurs. This study tests whether multi-hazard and machine-learning triggers reduce basis risk compared with simple wind triggers in Mozambique. We linked IBTrACS cyclone tracks, CHIRPS satellite-gauge rainfall, EM-DAT impacts, DesInventar records, African Risk Capacity post-event information and IMF World Economic Outlook data. Twenty-seven cyclone events were processed with one uniform rainfall method; 21 events with non-missing EM-DAT Total Affected values were used for classification. Four models were evaluated with leave-one-cyclone-out validation: a fixed 119 km/h wind trigger, a calibrated wind trigger, multihazard logistic regression and a random forest. The primary severe-impact threshold was 100,000 people affected. The two wind models had the lowest mismatch rate (19.0%), with 79.2% balanced accuracy and 91.7% recall. Logistic regression had 23.8% mismatch and random forest 28.6%. Results changed with impact threshold and rainfall corridor width. The findings show that added model complexity did not consistently reduce basis risk in this small, data-scarce sample. For practical product design, simple wind triggers remain strong benchmarks, and extra hazard variables should be retained only when they improve out-of-sample performance.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how AI progress affects capital allocation through financial information aggregation. Using institutional portfolio holdings, we document that manager pairs with greater common alignment with AI-extractable information subsequently hold more similar portfolios. Motivated by this evidence, we develop a model in which investors choose the quantity and composition of private and AI information, and firms learn from equilibrium asset prices before investing. A shared AI model error survives aggregation and enters prices, and investors may underestimate the overlap between AI information and prices. AI progress therefore changes both investors' information precision and prices' exposure to common errors. Cheaper access initially raises aggregate productivity when high costs keep AI use negligible, but further cost reductions can reverse the gain as AI research displaces private research. Improvements from very low model accuracy can instead lower productivity when increased reliance raises common-error exposure more than informed trading reduces noise-trader contamination. These results show how AI progress can expand investors' information acquisition while reducing the information prices convey to firms, worsening capital allocation even when firms use prices optimally.

detail.abstract: Observed multi-criteria choices are often interpreted retrospectively as evidence about which criterion mattered most. Classical value analysis has long emphasized that criterion weights depend on consequence ranges and value scales, and a separate literature has documented systematic effects of value-tree structure on elicited weights. Taking these results as established, this paper asks a different question: conditional on fixed value scales, which claims about criterion importance can an observed choice falsify? We distinguish two dimensions of criterion refinement. The first is whether the refined representation preserves the original additive utility model exactly or allows free reweighting of the new leaf criteria. The second is whether the importance claim is formulated at the branch level or at the leaf level of the value tree. For each of the four resulting representations, we derive in closed form the maximum compensation that the refined criterion can supply in support of a largest-weight hypothesis, which characterizes exactly when the hypothesis is falsified. Under utility-preserving refinement, the branch-level claim is invariant. The leaf-level claim, by contrast, is equivalent to a weaker statement whose strength is set by the largest refinement coefficient of the leaves. A sufficiently fine equal refinement therefore turns a largest-weight claim that is falsified in the unrefined tree into a rationalizable leaf-level claim, although the underlying utility model and the observed choice are unchanged and no elicitation bias is involved. We relate the result to the literatures on splitting bias, description invariance, importance information in criteria hierarchies, and preference disaggregation, and derive implications for interpreting criterion importance from observed choices.

In index and enhanced-index funds, which cannot discretionarily de-risk, every coefficient is null: the drawdown term is -0.000425 and the stress interaction -0.011371, and the difference between the two groups is significant. The amount beyond a dynamic threshold is significant out of sample, but pseudo-threshold and predictive-comparison tests identify no unique boundary and no forecasting advantage over static alternatives; every downstream result is shown to be invariant to replacing the dynamic rule with a static one or with raw drawdown. A 2014-2025 extension estimates a model-dependent population distribution of latent boundaries with a median near 6.5 percent, though the bootstrap interval for that median spans 3.5 to 21.0 percent and the tails remain imprecise and shock-dependent. In complete semiannual holdings, funds further beyond the threshold sell more of the same stock in stressed half-years (trade-weight interaction -0.00185, p = 0.026), although four of six trading measures show no significant stress interaction. A horse race against trailing cumulative returns shows that the conditional result is not separately identified from cumulative underperformance in this sample: the drawdown-by-stress term loses individual significance once a trailing-return interaction is present, and joint tests split between the two measures across history-length subsamples. detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether distance to the city center structures intra-urban inequality in Campinas, Brazil, a municipality of 1,139,047 inhabitants. Using 2022 Demographic Census universe data for all 2,592 census tracts, we measure the straight-line distance from each tract's residential centroid, derived from the Census address register (CNEFE), to a central landmark, Estação Cultura. With the same register, a reproducible procedure assigns neighborhood names to tracts (550 neighborhoods). We describe 16 indicators ring by ring and estimate tract-level Spearman correlations with distance.
333,939 people (29.3% of the population) live 10 km or more from the center. There, the median householder income is R$ 2,567, against R$ 3,791 within 10 km; the Black or brown population is 51.6% (against 34.2%), and 20.7% live in a favela or urban community (against 8.9%). Distance to the nearest health facility is the indicator most associated with distance to the center (ρ = 0.56). Household internet access, available only from the sample, reaches 92.0% of households but ranges from 79.8% to 97.7% across the 35 weighting areas, and it follows income (ρ = 0.68) more than distance (ρ = -0.42).
The gradient is neither continuous nor symmetric: high-income districts lie as far from the center as the poorest ones, so direction matters as much as distance. Distance is a lens on inequality, not an explanation of it. We release an interactive map and open data by tract and by neighborhood.
