detail.abstract: This paper is the second in a sub-series on the built environment and extends The Walls We Choose, which argued that the architect has been demoted from the person who helps people author the places they live to the person who makes a building comply. It asks what the body entrusted with the public interest in architecture did, while that happened. In Ontario, the Architects Act lends the profession the power to govern itself "in order that the public interest may be served and protected." The paper examines the public record of the Ontario Association of Architects from 2013 to 2026: its studies of site plan review, its letters and submissions to the province, its response to Bill 23, its governance, and the insurer it owns. The association measured the cost of reviewing design and never its value, until its figures became the province's case for ending the review. It took the profession's most consequential public positions without asking the profession. It requires every practice to buy mandatory insurance from a company it owns, on terms the members have never been asked to approve, while architects carry the liability for changes others require. detail.abstract: Competition among liquidity providers on Uniswap v3 and its successors is a lottery Colonel Blotto game. Providers divide capital across price ranges, and the fees earned in each range are split in proportion to the liquidity there. Measured in capital, ranges are battlefields and expected fees are prizes, which providers who disagree about where trading will occur value differently. Every position is public, so every player's allocation is observed. Equilibrium liquidity is determinate unless two providers' relative valuations of some pair of ranges differ by a factor of about 34 at equal capital. Because the equilibrium conditions invert, beliefs are identified up to scale from positions, and the threshold becomes a test. Across 1.1 million pairs of large providers and days in six Uniswap pools, the 99th percentile of disagreement is below a tenth of the threshold. Every crossing comes from a range far from the price on which one provider supplies nearly all the liquidity. Revealed beliefs predict where fees are earned near the price. In WETH/USDC, large providers nonetheless keep most of their capital far from the price, where it earns little but loses nothing to arbitrage. Measured swap by swap, their losses to arbitrage near the price are two thirds of loss-versus-rebalancing, and their allocation is nearly optimal given those losses. In USDC/USDT they keep less liquidity at the peg than their losses justify, as if insuring against a depeg. Unless beliefs are proportional, equilibrium liquidity generically has no formula in radicals.

detail.abstract: This paper asks whether the distance of price from a medium-horizon moving average, normalized by Average True Range (ATR), is more useful as a slow structural risk state than as a stand-alone directional trading signal. The slow state is defined as the prior trading day's close minus its 50-session simple moving average (SMA50), scaled by Wilder's 14-session ATR. This variable is combined with a fast intraday risk predictor based on recent realized volatility and evaluated primarily in E-mini S&P 500 (ES) and E-mini Nasdaq-100 (NQ) futures, with gold futures (GC) used as an additional mechanism check. The historical evidence is explicitly exploratory: the 2017-2019 and 2020-2023 periods were observed during iterative development and are not presented as independent confirmatory samples. Three results stand out. First, extreme ATR-normalized extension states are more consistently associated with larger future path ranges and higher realized volatility than with terminal directional displacement. Second, in ES, adding the lagged slow state to an already strong fast predictor improves LogLoss, the Brier score, and the area under the ROC curve (AUC); a minimal model consisting of fast state, slow state, and a single slow×fast interaction retains approximately 98% of the LogLoss improvement of a richer specification. Third, the interaction geometry replicates in NQ even though the slow main effect exhibits calibration drift. A causal Platt calibration re-estimated on the previous 60 trading sessions reduces LogLoss in both markets. The evidence supports a deliberately narrow interpretation: ATR-normalized price extension contains incremental information about the future state of risk, but does not by itself establish directional alpha or an economic edge. Later stages of the project froze a risk-management candidate for prospective evaluation; no post-freeze performance result is used in this article.

detail.abstract: Proposals to extend Taiwan's silicon shield from semiconductor fabrication into the verification of trusted computing infrastructure meet a legal question before a technical one. A trust regime runs on recognition: relying parties must accept, under their own law, results that someone else produced. Most governments do not recognize Taiwan as a state, and the principal arrangement for mutual acceptance of information-technology security certificates admits only government agencies representing countries. This Article shows that the obstacle is narrower than it appears. Taiwan already participates in rule-bound regimes through capacities defined by function rather than status: as a separate customs territory in the World Trade Organization and a party to the Agreement on Government Procurement, as a fishing entity in regional fisheries management, through agreements concluded by the American Institute in Taiwan and given domestic effect by the Taiwan Relations Act, and through an accreditation body that has been a signatory to the international laboratory accreditation arrangement since 2000. Conformity assessment is the most developed of these channels because it asks about competence rather than sovereignty. The same feature sets its limit. A route that admits bodies by attributes others can acquire secures eligibility, the standing of a Taiwanese body's results to count, without securing dependence, a partner's continued need for them. A Taiwanese laboratory could keep every recognition it holds and lose its customers to another accredited laboratory without any government acting. Legal reliance written into a partner's procurement rules can make exclusion reasoned and reviewable; it cannot prevent substitution. Continued importance depends on access to manufacturing evidence and independence in assessing it, and that access thins as fabrication and packaging move abroad. Stated generally, certification confers network power only when accepted evidence is non-fungible: necessary to the relying party and difficult to reproduce elsewhere. The Article proposes a design that protects eligibility through accreditation, a narrow procurement pilot, a withdrawal procedure with expiring emergency suspension, and continuity arrangements that preserve past evidence without transferring signing authority, and it states what that design cannot do.

title: When Is Text Data Valid？

detail.title: When Is Text Data Valid？

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Text is valid for economic measurement under conditions that are specific and checkable, and that much applied work does not check. I organize the literature around a measurement model in which a text-based variable is a noisy and possibly manipulated signal of a latent construct. Validity requires that the text be generated by the construct the theory names, that the mapping from construct to language be stable, that the remaining error be unrelated to the outcome, and that the signal survive in the variation that identifies the parameter. Simulations calibrated to a common application—artificial intelligence keywords in annual reports and firm hiring—show that a keyword count can be uninformative, or wrong-signed, when the underlying effect is large and a patent count detects it. Strategic disclosure elastic by only a few percent is enough. Context-aware classification, a second independent measure, and a hand-labeled validation sample restore most of what is lost

detail.abstract: The Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) and the Members Church of God International (MCGI) are doctrinal antagonists, yet the financial allegations against them run along parallel lines. Both churches have been accused of raising money under charitable or religious rationales, moving it across borders outside the reporting system, relying on members' labor and faith to do so, passing it through charities or businesses that give it a legitimate origin, and concentrating the resulting value in assets linked to their leaders. This essay compares the two cases using the U.S. federal indictment and related reporting on KOJC and its founder, Apollo Quiboloy, alongside an earlier forensic reconstruction of MCGI's media economy and the "disposable church" framework. It argues that the decisive difference lies in how each church deployed social capital. KOJC's alleged methods were concentrated: bulk cash on a private jet, a single U.S. charity that sent at least US$20 million to the Philippines, and labor that prosecutors say was obtained through coercion. MCGI's were distributed: a ₱1,200 monthly subscription called KAPI (Kabalikat sa Pamamahayag International) tied to fictitious insurance, concert pledges attached to zero-value tickets, cash divided among trusted travelers, and sales of a "hydrogen water" health product to members. Dispersal through a dense trust network kept each transaction small, unpaid, and internally policed, which made MCGI's model harder to detect than KOJC's.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the long-term impacts of a large temporary demand shock on regional industrialization. Specifically, I examine the Quartermaster sites through which the Union Army procured general manufactured goods during the U.S. Civil War, which were placed for wartime logistical reasons and dismantled when the war ended. Procurement had large and persistent effects on the host counties. Relative to comparison counties, manufacturing employment and population expanded significantly after 1860, and by 1890 the QM counties had 66 percent more manufacturing employment and a population 19 percent larger. The manufacturing lead persisted at about this level until the 1960s and then declined with the national contraction of manufacturing, while the population lead persisted. The persistent expansion came through persistent adoption of new industries by treated counties, and counties became less farm-dependent earlier. A quantitative spatial model in which procurement raised a county's rate of adopting new techniques rationalizes the empirical findings and implies that procurement raised Union real income per worker by 5.9 percent by 1940.

detail.abstract: The mapping from option-implied risk-neutral crash probabilities to physical probabilities depends on how systematic crash risk is. We develop an option-implied lower bound using only the firm's own option smile and historical returns. A firm-specific systematicity parameter governs the adjustment: more idiosyncratic crash risk keeps the bound closer to the risk-neutral probability, while more systematic crash risk moves it toward the Martin and Shi (2026) benchmark. Illustrative diffusion and jump economies show that the implementable bound closely tracks true physical crash probabilities. Empirically, our bound adds substantial predictive information beyond the Martin-Shi benchmark among firms with high idiosyncratic risk and delivers stronger out-of-sample forecasts at medium and longer horizons, consistent with the theoretical prediction.

detail.abstract: When a first judicial auction fails in China, the court may lower the starting price for the second auction. A larger reduction may attract bidders, but it may also reflect information that the property is difficult to sell. Using 2025 real estate listings from Alibaba Judicial Auctions, we construct 171,447 matched first-and second-auction pairs from 628,566 listings after excluding bankruptcy and compulsory liquidation sales, reauctions after bidder default, and third or later auctions. The second-auction sale rate is 25.10%. In a linear probability model controlling for the first-auction starting price, first-auction viewer count, and month fixed effects, the coefficient on the starting-price discount is-1.4659. Thus, a 10 percentage point increase in the discount is associated with a 14.66 percentage point decline in sale probability. The distribution is concentrated at the 20% ceiling: 42.84% of pairs receive this discount, and their sale rate is 14.27%. Within the 5%-18% range, however, a 10 percentage point increase is associated with a 1.28 percentage point rise in sale probability. The overall negative association remains under alternative matching screens, sample restrictions, treatments of viewer counts, and probit estimation. Because courts choose the discount after the failed first auction, the estimates are interpreted as conditional correlations rather than causal effects.

detail.abstract:
The foundational principle of international commercial arbitration resides in party consent. However, modern global commerce is increasingly dominated by intricate multi-layered corporate structures, multi-party supply chains, and complex transnational conglomerates, creating a fundamental tension between the formal privity of contract and economic commercial reality. This paper undertakes a doctrinal, comparative, and jurisprudential analysis of the legal mechanisms deployed to bind non-signatory entities to arbitration agreements, with a focused critique on the “Group of Companies” doctrine.

Originating in the seminal Dow Chemical award, the doctrine posits that an arbitration clause signed by one group member may extend to non-signatory corporate affiliates that substantially participated in the negotiation, performance, or termination of the underlying contract. This study criticallyevaluates the divergent approaches across key arbitral seats—contrasting the proactive pro-arbitration stance of French and Indian jurisprudence (notably following the landmark Cox and Kings Ltd v. SAP India ruling) against the strict adherence to privity maintained by English common law and Swiss courts. Furthermore, the paper delineates the theoretical boundaries separating implied consent from equitable doctrines such as alter ego/piercing the corporate veil, agency, and estoppel. The article concludes by formulating a harmonized procedural framework that balances the commercial imperative of single-forum dispute resolution against the imperative protection of party autonomy and the enforceable integrity of arbitral awards under Article II and V of the New York Convention.

detail.abstract: Managers' discount rates often diverge from market-implied costs of capital. detail.abstract: This paper develops a revised framework for studying the relationship between economic complexity and domestic competition. The central argument is that productive complexity can affect competition through two opposing mechanisms. A capability-rich economy can widen the set of technologically feasible activities, deepen specialized input markets, and support entry into related activities; at the same time, complex production can raise fixed capability requirements, sunk costs, coordination burdens, and minimum efficient scale, thereby screening entrants and reducing market churn. The net relationship between economic complexity and competition is therefore theoretically ambiguous and may be nonlinear. We distinguish realized market competition—entry, exit, churn, concentration, and markups—from institutional conditions that facilitate competition. This distinction is crucial because broad economic-freedom indices are not direct measures of competition. We propose a country-year panel design combining the Economic Complexity Index with competition outcomes and institutional measures, with country and year fixed effects, nonlinear specifications, and explicit treatment of endogeneity. Recent evidence on European firm dynamics, showing that higher complexity can reduce entry and churn, reinforces the need to move beyond the simple hypothesis that more complex economies are necessarily more competitive. The revised framework yields testable hypotheses about market dynamism, barriers to entry, institutional moderation, and nonlinearities, and provides a more rigorous basis for evaluating the competition consequences of structural transformation.

These shocks forced the Kalman lter into extreme belief updating, highlighting the vulnerability of adaptive learning mechanisms and demonstrating that the loss of ination control was not purely a deliberate policy choice.

detail.abstract: Liquidity premia are measured from outside: through reversal portfolios an econometrician constructs, through price-impact coefficients, or through inventory effects inferred from quotes. detail.abstract: The order in which teachers and other staff gather evidence, and the order of questions on an incident form, can change whether a behaviour is read as a sign of need or as conduct. That reading determines if the child moves towards SEN support or towards behaviour sanction, and for non-verbal pupils who cannot say what they feel, it is often the first step in SEND identification. Research on SEND judgment over the last four decades has shown variation in cases but little to nothing on how the order in which staff meet cues, or the order of questions on an incident form, influences that reading. This paper treats both sequences as design variables and proposes quantum probability, in its narrow mathematical sense, as a way to test them. Classical models explain order effects by weighting early or late evidence differently. Quantum probability, on the other hand, builds order into the rules: answering one question changes the state from which the next is answered, so when two questions do not commute, swapping them changes the joint pattern of yes and no answers. The model also predicts the QQ equality, a parameter-free constraint that held across 70 nationally representative surveys. This paper proposes a vignette study to separate the accounts. Cue order is tested by comparing the fit of quantum and classical models. Question order is tested by swapping two yes/no items and asking whether the QQ equality holds. A one-question control tests whether answering the first question changes the answer to the second. Four predictions follow, including that order effects shrink with professional experience and differ between teachers and occupational therapists. The argument extends to referral for statutory SEN assessment.

detail.abstract: A decision maker who acts on an AI's recommendation without first forming her own judgment learns how accurate the AI is, but not how accurate she would have been. We study a forwardlooking agent who, in each period, decides whether to form her own judgment at a cost before seeing the AI's recommendation, with her ability held fixed. When the AI's accuracy is known, this is an optimal stopping problem with a cutoff in self-confidence. Capable agents stop judging independently with positive probability and remain underconfident about their own type, while incapable agents eventually defer. The probability of this lock-in is weakly higher when human errors reproduce more of the AI's error, holding the human's idiosyncratic error fixed, or when the AI is more accurate, since both reduce the value of independent judgment without changing what it reveals. Lock-in persists when the AI's accuracy is unknown, because experience corrects beliefs about the AI but not about oneself. An agent who is averse to ambiguity about the frequency of capable agents behaves like a Bayesian with a pessimistic prior. For a designer who knows that frequency, disclosing it alone lowers welfare near full human competence when the AI is better than the agent believes, and raises it when the AI is worse. Random audits of unaided work crowd out voluntary independent judgment, and even mandates targeted at the right periods leave the agent underweighting her own judgment.

detail.abstract: AI-2040 "Plan A," published by the AI Futures Project in 2026, is becoming the working template for a US-China agreement on advanced AI. A plan of that consequence should be checked the way an engineer checks a safety-critical design before it is built, not judged on its rhetoric. This paper does that, using the tools of the Governance Operating System (GOS). It decomposes Plan A into its mechanisms, maps the interface each one depends on, sets a baseline of what must stay controlled, and tests the design in both directions: forward (does it work, and under what conditions) and backward (what produces the danger it is meant to govern). The finding is that Plan A is capability-dependent and deal-dependent; its load-bearing conditions are weak or self-contradictory; and in the end it must trust the machine. The paper then sets out the alternative: a trust-free accord built on GOS, in which each sovereign enforces one common actuation standard at home-the same pattern of standards harmonization that already works in civil aviation, banking, and nuclear safeguards. The alternative is acceptable to the United States and China, to industry, to other states, and to users, because it asks none of them to trust, to slow, or to reveal. It is objective, simple, andlow-cost, and it does not force the world toward an outcome no one yet knows how to secure. The paper names the cause, prescribes the cure, and estimates the result.

detail.abstract: Order-level data from exchanges is often restricted or costly, which makes it hard for independent researchers to build a synthetic limit order book for the venue they study. This paper shows how to build a venue-specific generator from public sources alone: published research, exchange statistics, and regulator reports. The method has four steps. We write a profile of the venue's trading day, turn its published statistics into numeric targets, add mechanisms one at a time, and check each mechanism directly. Using the Nikkei 225 mini futures on the Osaka Exchange as a worked example, the resulting generator meets 13 required targets on the five synthetic days used for calibration and, under the same pass rules, on 20 further days. Trades did not move the price until that was built in; a standard impact measure passed by measuring trades that follow price moves; the price impact of trades did not fade without a slow mechanism; and the branching ratio estimated from trades understated its true value, partly through the order book and partly through the estimation procedure. detail.abstract: International education is still sold as a degree, but what families now buy is closer to an option: a claim on future residency, work rights, and professional recognition that can be cancelled after the money is spent. This paper argues that the international degree has at least two counterparties able to revoke its value unilaterally, the host state that controls access to the training and the home regulator that controls whether the qualification counts, and that a third force, the rapid redrawing of entry-level labor markets by artificial intelligence, now erodes the destination without anyone revoking anything. Families cannot price these risks because international education is a credence good whose quality is revealed years after purchase. The intermediaries who guide the purchase, education agents paid at enrolment by institutions and often by families as well, carry none of the risk that materializes afterwards, a timing mismatch structurally similar to the originate-todistribute incentive problem in pre-2008 mortgage lending. The argument is developed through documented episodes: the stranding of more than 23,000 Indian medical students by China's pandemic border closure and India's refusal to recognize online-only training; the Ukraine evacuation; the 2025 to 2026 tightening of student visa regimes in the United States and Canada; the deregulation of China's agent market and the absence of national agent regulation in India; the published standards of the main agent certification body; patterns observed in one South Asian consultancy's public promotional material; and the rapid growth of foreign branch campuses in Uzbekistan. Transnational education, which brings the degree to the student, removes the visa counterparty but introduces another: the foreign institution that can withdraw. The paper closes with design principles for rebalancing the risk, including deferred commissions, ownership disclosure, sending-state regulation, and a portable student-held record, and sets out a research agenda for Central Asia, where agent markets are growing with almost no published scrutiny.

detail.abstract: Qualitative research is collecting, analyzing, and interpreting subjective data to answer an important research question. It can be contrasted with quantitative research, which focuses on collecting numerical (relatively objective) data to test specific hypotheses. It is an attractive form of research in church contexts because it does not require training in statistics and can be conducted in almost all ministry settings. It is especially appropriate for topics that are under-researched, poorly understood, or involve concepts that are difficult to measure. Common problems associated with church-based qualitative research include overly broad research questions, weak descriptions of what has been observed, shallow analysis, and biased interpretation. Qualitative studies that are the most useful will include the collection of high-quality data (typically from interviews) that reaches saturation, thick descriptions, and reflexivity and transparency about the researcher's biases and values. Five forms of qualitative studies are described: narrative, phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, and case study. All forms of qualitative research can generate important insights and practical applications for ministry settings if they are based on high-quality data and analyzed in depth.

detail.abstract: Business model innovation (BMI) has long been understood as a periodic, deliberate exercise in redesigning how organisations create, deliver, and capture value. The growing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) in organisational life is beginning to unsettle that assumption. Predictive analytics, machine learning, and generative systems allow firms to sense market signals and adjust operations in near real time, which raises the question of whether BMI is becoming a continuous, algorithmically mediated process rather than an episodic one. This paper offers an integrative review of the management, information systems, and strategic innovation literatures to examine how AI is reshaping the theory and practice of BMI. Following the methodological guidance of Whittemore and Knafl (2005) and Torraco (2005), the review synthesises conceptual and empirical work published across leading journals to build a thematic picture of AI-driven value creation, value delivery, and value capture. The analysis shows that while the technical capabilities of AI are well documented, their strategic integration into coherent business models remains fragmented, with most studies treating AI as a tool bolted onto existing structures rather than as a force that reorganises the logic of the business model itself. The review develops a matrix of AI capability archetypes, identifies recurring organisational and ethical tensions, and proposes practical implications for managers and policymakers. It closes with an agenda for future research organised by methodology, context, and level of analysis, intended to guide scholars toward a more integrated theory of AI-enabled business model transformation.

detail.abstract: Decision support systems for capacity-constrained logistics networks traditionally require dedicated engineering teams, infrastructure investment, and long development cycles, creating an execution gap between domain expertise and operational analytical tools. This paper presents the design and a synthetic-data evaluation of a serverless, schedule-triggered decision support architecture built with a multi-agent AI development method. The architecture comprises a primary AI agent supported by multiple specialized agents, four scheduled AWS Lambda data pipelines (Python 3.12) triggered daily via Amazon EventBridge, an S3 data lake protected with Origin Access Control, a CloudFront content delivery network, and a client-side multi-criteria computation engine that executes ranking logic in the browser without an application server. A reference implementation of the two-stage scoring logic is evaluated on a synthetic dataset of 1,500 entity records in six tiers, generated for this study (the generator is available from the authors on request), under 1,000 Dirichlet-sampled weight vectors, three weight scenarios, and 20 replication datasets. Tier boundaries were never violated (0 of 1,000 draws), mean within-tier displacement was about 10% of tier size, and the baseline top Tier-1 entity stayed within the top three positions in 99.4% of draws in the main dataset (mean 0.899 over 20 replications). A design-time cost estimate, computed from published AWS pricing and free-tier limits, places steady-state compute, storage, and CDN cost at approximately $0 to under $5 per month under stated assumptions; load and recomputation times are stated as design targets, not measurements. No field deployment, user study, or productivity measurement is reported. In this paper, "real-time" refers to interactive in-browser recomputation; data refresh is a daily batch process, and the AI agents act at build time under human approval. This paper contributes: (1) a serverless architecture pattern for decision support that needs no application server, with an estimated cost model; (2) a qualitatively documented multi-agent build method; (3) a multi-agent specialization model (multiple domain-specific agents plus one primary orchestration agent); and (4) design principles for client-side computation in high-entity-count analytical systems, with a synthetic-data evaluation of the scoring logic. detail.abstract: Weighted multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) models are widely used in logistics operations, yet reports of rigorous validation of ranking stability under weight uncertainty remain rare. This paper presents a Monte Carlo simulation framework for validating the robustness of two-stage weighted scoring models applied to entity prioritization in large-scale logistics distribution networks, and demonstrates it on a synthetic dataset of 1,500 entity-location records (entities evaluated at specific facility locations) generated for this study. The dataset, the generator and all reported results are synthetic: they demonstrate method behavior and are not empirical estimates for any real network. Using 1,000 stochastic weight perturbations (Dirichlet-sampled) over four active criteria-Cost Effectiveness (a normalized cost-efficiency measure), outbound transportation capacity, facility handling capacity, and delivery performance, with operational compliance held out as unpopulated, consistent with [1]-we verify that a two-stage architecture (categorical tier pre-sort followed by continuous weighted scoring) produces zero cross-tier ranking violations in all 1,000 scenarios, a design property that follows from using the tier as the primary sort key. The substantive evidence concerns within-tier stability. In the main synthetic draw, the baseline topranked Tier-1 entity remained within the top three absolute positions in 99.4% of the perturbations (and held rank 1 in 78.1%), but across 20 further synthetic datasets this top-three retention averaged 89.9% (range 56.7% to 100%), so it is dataset-dependent. Mean within-tier displacement was about 10% of tier size in every tier (mean withintier Spearman correlation with the baseline ordering of 0.88 to 0.89). detail.abstract:
The institutionalization of Third-Party Funding (TPF) has recalibrated the economic and procedural equilibrium of international commercial and investment treaty arbitration. While non-recourse dispute financing serves as a formidable mechanism for access to justice and corporate risk hedging, the presence of an undisclosed commercial entity with an economic stake in the award introduces systemic hazards to the arbitral process. Chief among these are unvetted arbitrator conflicts of interest, asymmetrical repeat-player phenomena, threats to legal privilege, and the procedural risk of unrecoverable adverse cost awards against non-signatory entities.This paper critically analyzes the paradigm shift from traditional common law prohibitions (maintenance and champerty) toward sophisticated, codificatory disclosure regimes. By examining the transformative provisions of the 2022 ICSID Arbitration Rules (Rule 14), the 2021 ICC Arbitration Rules (Article 11(7)), and the newly revised 2024 IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration—which formally assimilate third-party funders to commercial parties—the study delineates the exact normative boundaries between mandatory identity disclosure and the preservation of confidential funding terms.

Furthermore, the paper deconstructs prevailing arbitral jurisprudence concerning applications for security for costs, demonstrating that while funding does not warrant a per se presumption ofimpecuniosity, it justifies heightened scrutiny where structural asset-shielding exists. Ultimately, the article advocates for a harmonized, multi-tiered regulatory framework that enforces strict transparency to uphold procedural integrity while insulating party autonomy and settlement authority from undue funder control.

detail.abstract:
The international arbitral process relies fundamentally on the principle of negative competence-competence, obligating national courts to decline jurisdiction in favor of an agreed arbitral forum pursuant to Article II(3) of the 1958 New York Convention. However, recalcitrant parties frequently initiate parallel, vexatious, or oppressive litigation in foreign domestic courts to frustrate arbitral proceedings, exploit localized procedural advantages, or obtain conflicting substantive judgments. To protect the sanctity and exclusivity of the arbitration agreement, national courts at the seat of arbitration—principally in common law jurisdictions—frequently deploy Anti-Suit Injunctions (ASIs) to restrain parties subject to their in personam jurisdiction from prosecuting foreign court actions in breach of their negative covenants.

This paper provides a doctrinal and comparative critique of the normativefoundation, procedural mechanics, and transnational validity of ASIs in international commercial dispute resolution. It analyzes the fundamental tension between the judicial enforcement of contractual dispute resolution clauses and the principles of international comity (comitas gentium) and state sovereignty. The study conducts a comparative assessment across key arbitral centers: the proactive, equitable approach of English and Commonwealth courts (contrasting historical EU restrictions under the West Tankers doctrine with the post-Brexit revival of judicial enforcement powers in the United Kingdom), the emerging jurisprudence of emergency arbitrators issuing arbitral anti-suit measures under institutional rules, and the systemic resistance maintained by civil law jurisdictions (notably France and Switzerland) which view ASIs as impermissible extraterritorial interferences. Finally, the paper evaluates the enforceability and recognition of awards rendered pursuant to ASIs under the New York Convention and proposes an objective, harmonized standard to distinguishlegitimate contractual enforcement from abusive jurisdictional aggression.

Capable agents stop judging independently with positive probability and remain underconfident about their own type, while incapable agents eventually defer. The probability of this lock-in is weakly higher when human errors reproduce more of the AI's error, holding the human's idiosyncratic error fixed, or when the AI is more accurate, since both reduce the value of independent judgment without changing what it reveals. Lock-in persists when the AI's accuracy is unknown, because experience corrects beliefs about the AI but not about oneself. An agent who is averse to ambiguity about the frequency of capable agents behaves like a Bayesian with a pessimistic prior. For a designer who knows that frequency, disclosing it alone lowers welfare near full human competence when the AI is better than the agent believes, and raises it when the AI is worse. Random audits of unaided work crowd out voluntary independent judgment, and even mandates targeted at the right periods leave the agent underweighting her own judgment.

detail.abstract: When shortage and excess penalties are quadratic, the newsvendor's optimal order is an expectile of demand, not the critical fractile. We ask what ordering at the fractile costs. For any demand with finite variance, the fractile costs at most twice the optimum, and the factor of two is attained at every cost ratio. In absolute terms the excess is at most (c u + c o)σ 2 /4, where 1 2 c u and 1 2 c o weight the mean squared shortage and excess; this is again tight, and a companion inequality bounds the quantile-expectile distance by σ/(2 q(1-q)). When only the mean and variance are known, the quadratic analogue of Scarf's (1958) min-max rule is to order the mean, or a closed-form smaller amount when demand is non-negative and excess is the costlier error. For log-concave demand we adapt the localization theorem of Fradelizi and Guédon (2004) to show that the worst case is approached by truncated exponential densities; a certified computation then bounds the excess by 31.42% of the optimum for critical ratios in [0.1, 0.9] and 36.85% in [0.005, 0.995]. Unimodality alone helps much less: the worst unimodal demand is approached by mixtures of at most two uniforms anchored at the mode, one possibly degenerate, and at the certified cost ratios the excess is 60-65%. The reverse mistake, the expectile used under linear penalties, also costs at most twice the optimum, but log-concavity does not bound it away from two at extreme cost ratios.

detail.abstract: Digital agriculture may alter the farm size-productivity relationship by making effective technology use increasingly dependent on operated area, accumulated data, and technological compatibility. This paper examines whether scale-biased digitalization can overturn the traditional inverse relationship between farm size and land productivity and generate cumulative land concentration. A parsimonious socio-physical simulation links heterogeneous farm size, digital-use intensity, cumulative data capital, readiness, productivity, risk-adjusted competitiveness, and land reallocation. The framework uses stylized benchmark parameters to isolate the underlying feedback mechanism. Digital scale bias and interoperability jointly determine the effective advantage associated with farm size. A sufficiently strong scaledependent advantage can offset and reverse the inverse productivity gradient, while greater interoperability raises the digital-use intensity required for reversal. Structural concentration becomes substantial mainly when pronounced digital scale bias is combined with responsive land markets. These outcomes are conditional on the adopted mechanisms and parameterization. The central implication is that the structural consequences of digitalization depend on how data move across systems and how performance differences feed into land access. This result shows why assessments of digital transformation should consider technological architecture, data portability, and farm-structure adjustment alongside average productivity gains.

detail.abstract:
The practice of “double-hatting”—wherein a legal practitioner simultaneously or consecutively acts as an arbitrator and as counsel or expert in concurrent or related disputes involving overlapping factual or legal questions—represents one of the most contentious ethical dilemmas in international arbitration. While proponents argue that dual practice expands the pool of qualified specialists and enriches procedural sophistication, critics contend that it structurally undermines arbitrator independence, creates cognitive confirmation biases, and fosters irreconcilable issue conflicts. This article examines the conceptual evolution of double-hatting across international commercial arbitration and investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS). It analyses the emerging regulatory landscape, focusing on the 2023 UNCITRAL/ICSID Code of Conduct for Adjudicators and the 2024 Revisions to the IBA
Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in International Arbitration. The study investigates the resulting annulment and enforcement vulnerabilities under Articles V(1)(d) and V(2)(b) of the 1958 New York Convention, arguing that systemic arbitral legitimacy requires mandatory disclosure protocols, temporal cooling-off periods, and clear institutional firewalls.
